questions.q: Which 1947 policy pledged American support to free peoples resisting communist pressure and began with aid to Greece and Turkey?
options: The Monroe Doctrine
The Eisenhower Doctrine
The Truman Doctrine
The Roosevelt Corollary
questions.explain: Truman asked Congress for money for Greece and Turkey, and the idea of backing states that resisted communist pressure became the core of containment.

questions.q: The Marshall Plan, begun in 1948, was mainly designed to do what?
options: Rebuild Western European economies with American aid
Fund a United Nations army to defend South Korea
Resettle displaced European refugees in American cities
Collect repayment of Allied war debts from Europe
questions.explain: The European Recovery Program sent billions of dollars to Western Europe, aiming to restore trade and stability and reduce the appeal of communism.

questions.q: George Kennan's 1947 article signed "X" in Foreign Affairs is best known for laying out which strategy toward the Soviet Union?
options: Rollback
Containment
Massive retaliation
Appeasement
questions.explain: Kennan argued the United States should apply firm, patient pressure to stop Soviet expansion, and the idea shaped policy for decades.

questions.q: What was the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, created in 1949?
options: A trade bloc that removed tariffs among Atlantic nations
A court for settling legal disputes between European states
An economic aid agency distributing American grants to Europe
A military alliance in which members pledged collective defense
questions.explain: NATO members agreed that an armed attack on one would be treated as an attack on all, tying the United States to Europe's defense in peacetime.

questions.q: How did the United States and Britain respond when the Soviets blockaded West Berlin in 1948?
options: They sent tank columns down the highways to break it
They withdrew their troops and recognized Soviet control
They negotiated a deal transferring Berlin to East Germany
They flew in food and fuel in the Berlin Airlift
questions.explain: Planes supplied the city for about a year; the Soviets lifted the blockade in May 1949 without having forced the Western powers out.

questions.q: The Korean War began in June 1950 when which event occurred?
options: Chinese troops crossed the Yalu River into South Korea and attacked
American planes bombed Pyongyang and the Yalu River bridges
North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel into South Korea
Soviet forces crossed the 38th parallel into South Korea
questions.explain: North Korea's attack across the 38th parallel prompted the UN Security Council to back military aid to South Korea.

questions.q: Why was the UN Security Council able to authorize a military response to the invasion of South Korea in June 1950?
options: The General Assembly overrode the Soviet veto under a special procedure
The Soviet delegate was boycotting the council and did not veto it
Every permanent member, including the Soviet Union, voted in favor
The United States held the presidency and set aside the veto rule
questions.explain: The Soviet Union was absent in protest over China's seat, so it could not use its veto against the resolutions on Korea.

questions.q: What was the result of General Douglas MacArthur's amphibious landing at Inchon in September 1950?
options: It cut North Korean supply lines and allowed UN forces to retake Seoul
It trapped the American Eighth Army against the Yalu River until winter
It ended the fighting with an armistice along the 38th parallel
It drew China into the war and forced UN forces out of Seoul
questions.explain: The surprise landing behind enemy lines turned the war around and UN forces then pushed north across the 38th parallel.

questions.q: What led China to enter the Korean War in late 1950?
options: UN forces advanced toward the Yalu River on China's border
The United States dropped an atomic bomb on Manchuria
South Korean troops raided Chinese territory in Manchuria
The Soviet Union ordered China to send troops under its command
questions.explain: As American-led forces neared the Yalu, Chinese troops attacked in large numbers and drove the UN army back south.

questions.q: Why did President Truman remove General MacArthur from command in April 1951?
options: MacArthur's forces had been routed at the Inchon landing
MacArthur announced a campaign for the presidency in 1952
MacArthur publicly challenged the policy of limiting the war
MacArthur lost the confidence of Congress over war profiteering
questions.explain: Truman held that civilian leaders set policy; MacArthur's open calls to widen the war to China conflicted with that principle.

questions.q: How did the fighting in the Korean War end in July 1953?
options: With a peace treaty that reunited Korea under one government
With an armistice that left Korea divided near the 38th parallel
With the unconditional surrender of North Korea to UN forces
With a Chinese withdrawal followed by nationwide elections
questions.explain: The armistice halted combat and created a demilitarized zone but no formal peace treaty, so the peninsula stayed divided.

questions.q: NSC-68, a 1950 national security paper, recommended which course for the United States?
options: A return to prewar isolation from European affairs
Disarmament talks with Moscow to reduce nuclear arms
A retreat from NATO commitments to cut defense costs
A large buildup of American military strength
questions.explain: The paper urged much higher defense spending to counter the Soviet Union, and the Korean War helped win acceptance for it.

questions.q: Which communist-bloc alliance formed in 1955 as a Soviet response to NATO?
options: The Comintern alliance
The Axis alliance
The SEATO alliance
The Warsaw Pact
questions.explain: After West Germany joined NATO, the Soviet Union and its Eastern European allies signed the Warsaw Pact.

questions.q: In a 1946 speech at Fulton, Missouri, Winston Churchill said an "iron curtain" had descended across what?
options: Asia
The Atlantic Ocean
Europe
The Middle East
questions.explain: Churchill's phrase described the Soviet-dominated division of the continent, and it became a common label for the early Cold War.

questions.q: President Truman's Executive Order 9981 in 1948 did what?
options: Ordered an end to segregation in the armed forces
Banned racial discrimination in private hiring nationwide
Required desegregation of public schools in Washington
Banned poll taxes in federal elections across the South
questions.explain: The order called for equal treatment in the military; full integration took years and was hastened by the manpower needs of the Korean War.

questions.q: The House Un-American Activities Committee investigated which group in 1947 and cited some of its witnesses for contempt?
options: Labor union presidents in the steel industry accused of sabotage
Hollywood screenwriters and directors accused of communist ties
Officers of the Federal Reserve accused of favoring Moscow
State Department diplomats accused of leaking atomic secrets
questions.explain: Ten witnesses from the film industry refused to answer questions and were jailed, and studios then blacklisted many people.

questions.q: Which senator gained national fame in 1950 by claiming that communists had infiltrated the State Department?
options: Estes Kefauver
Robert Taft
Barry Goldwater
Joseph McCarthy
questions.explain: McCarthy's speech at Wheeling, West Virginia, launched a campaign of accusations; his name later gave the label McCarthyism to such tactics.

questions.q: What ended Senator McCarthy's influence in the mid-1950s?
options: The televised Army-McCarthy hearings and a Senate censure in 1954
His defeat for reelection to the Senate in the 1952 election
A Supreme Court ruling that his committee was unconstitutional
His expulsion from the Senate by a two-thirds vote in 1954
questions.explain: Viewers saw his aggressive questioning on television during the 1954 hearings, and the Senate then voted to censure him.

questions.q: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were executed in 1953 after being convicted of what?
options: Selling stolen military aircraft designs to Nazi Germany
Conspiring to pass atomic secrets to the Soviet Union
Bribing members of Congress to oppose the Marshall Plan
Leaking Manhattan Project plans to Japan during the war
questions.explain: Their trial came as Americans feared Soviet atomic spying, and their case remained part of the debate over Cold War fears.

questions.q: In Dennis v. United States (1951), the Supreme Court upheld convictions of Communist Party leaders under which law?
options: The Sedition Act of 1798
The Espionage Act of 1917
The Smith Act
The Taft-Hartley Act
questions.explain: The Court held that the Smith Act, which banned advocating violent overthrow of the government, could be applied to the party's leaders.

questions.q: What did the Soviet launch of Sputnik in October 1957 prompt in the United States?
options: A new emphasis on science education and the founding of NASA
A treaty with Moscow banning military satellites in orbit
A cut in defense budgets to pay for domestic programs
A joint American-Soviet space agency run through the UN
questions.explain: Americans feared falling behind in technology, leading to the National Defense Education Act of 1958 and the creation of NASA that year.

questions.q: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) was created in what year?
questions.explain: Congress passed the National Aeronautics and Space Act in 1958, the year after Sputnik, to organize a civilian space program.

questions.q: Explorer 1, launched on January 31, 1958, was significant as what?
options: The first American crewed orbital flight
The first American satellite in orbit
The first probe sent to the moon
The first reconnaissance satellite in orbit
questions.explain: The satellite answered Sputnik and carried an experiment that helped reveal the Van Allen radiation belts.

questions.q: In his 1961 farewell address, what did President Eisenhower warn Americans to guard against?
options: The rapid expansion of the Soviet navy in the Atlantic
A return to isolationism and the abandonment of allies
The unwarranted influence of the military-industrial complex
The rising cost of the interstate highway system program
questions.explain: Eisenhower, a former general, cautioned that a permanent arms industry joined with the military could threaten democratic government.

questions.q: The "domino theory" held that what would happen if one Southeast Asian country fell to communism?
options: Soviet influence would fade across the region
China would abandon communism and trade with the West
Allied governments would gain stronger security
Neighboring countries would likely follow
questions.explain: Eisenhower described the idea in 1954, and later presidents used it to justify involvement in Vietnam.

questions.q: The Eisenhower Doctrine of 1957 pledged American help to which region?
options: Latin American governments threatened by communist coups
Southeast Asian nations threatened by communist insurgency
Middle Eastern nations threatened by communist aggression
Eastern European nations threatened by Soviet domination
questions.explain: Congress authorized the president to use force or aid in the Middle East after the Suez Crisis showed a shifting balance of power there.

questions.q: During the Suez Crisis of 1956, how did the Eisenhower administration respond to the attack by Britain, France, and Israel on Egypt?
options: It pressured the three nations to withdraw
It sent naval forces to support the attack
It stayed neutral and refused to act at the UN
It offered to mediate while backing the invasion
questions.explain: The United States opposed the invasion at the UN and applied economic pressure, a split among Western allies that Moscow tried to exploit.

questions.q: In 1953 the CIA helped to remove the prime minister of which country, Mohammad Mossadegh?
options: Egypt
Iran
Guatemala
Cuba
questions.explain: Mossadegh had nationalized the British-controlled oil industry; a coup restored the shah, and the episode later fed anti-American feeling in Iran.

questions.q: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956, which created the interstate highway system, was defended by supporters partly because of what?
options: The need to compete with Canadian trade routes
Its value for national defense and evacuation
Plans to phase out railroad subsidies nationwide
Fears of a national shortage of oil supplies
questions.explain: It was officially named the National System of Interstate and Defense Highways and encouraged car travel and suburban growth.

questions.q: What was the U-2 incident of May 1960?
options: A Chinese missile shot down an American spy plane over Manchuria
A U-2 pilot defected to Moscow with secret photographs of bases
A Soviet missile shot down an American spy plane and captured its pilot
A U-2 strayed over Cuba and was shot down by Castro's air defenses
questions.explain: The capture of pilot Francis Gary Powers embarrassed Eisenhower and helped sink a Paris summit with Khrushchev.

questions.q: The Bay of Pigs invasion of April 1961 was an attempt to do what?
options: Overthrow Fidel Castro using Cuban exiles trained by the CIA
Capture a Soviet submarine base on Cuba's northern coast
Rescue American citizens held hostage by Castro's regime
Install a pro-American government in Haiti using exiles
questions.explain: The exiles were defeated within days, a setback for the new Kennedy administration.

questions.q: What evidence led President Kennedy to announce a naval quarantine of Cuba in October 1962?
options: Cuban jets attacked American air bases in Florida without warning
The Soviet Union announced a naval blockade of Florida ports
Khrushchev announced at the UN that missiles were aimed at Texas
U-2 photographs showed Soviet missile sites under construction in Cuba
questions.explain: U-2 photographs showed Soviet missile sites under construction; Kennedy told the nation on October 22 and announced a naval quarantine of Cuba.

questions.q: How was the Cuban Missile Crisis resolved?
options: The United States invaded the island and the Soviets withdrew their forces
The Soviets removed the missiles and the United States pledged not to invade Cuba
Cuba agreed to hold elections under UN supervision and Soviet troops left
Castro expelled Soviet advisers and the United States lifted its embargo
questions.explain: Khrushchev agreed to pull out the missiles; the United States also quietly agreed to withdraw missiles from Turkey later.

questions.q: The Berlin Wall, built in August 1961, was constructed by East Germany mainly to do what?
options: Protect East Berlin from Allied bombing raids
Mark the boundary of a newly independent state
Keep Western spies out of East German cities
Stop East Germans from fleeing to West Berlin
questions.explain: Many skilled East Germans had left through Berlin; the wall sealed the border and became a symbol of the Cold War division.

questions.q: What did the Limited Test Ban Treaty of 1963 prohibit?
options: All nuclear tests of any kind, including underground explosions
The deployment of missiles with ranges over 500 miles
Nuclear tests in the atmosphere, outer space, and underwater
Reconnaissance satellites over the territory of rival nations
questions.explain: The United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union agreed to stop testing everywhere except underground, a step toward easing tensions after the Cuban Missile Crisis.

questions.q: The "hotline" installed between Washington and Moscow in 1963 was meant to do what?
options: Allow leaders to communicate quickly during a crisis
Broadcast American radio news across the Iron Curtain
Connect the Senate directly to NATO headquarters
Let intelligence agents send coded messages in Berlin
questions.explain: The Cuban Missile Crisis showed that slow communication risked war, and the direct link was created to prevent misjudgment.

questions.q: Which program, created by President Kennedy in 1961, sent American volunteers abroad to help developing countries?
options: The Job Corps
The Marshall Plan
The Alliance for Progress
The Peace Corps
questions.explain: The Peace Corps sought to promote friendship and aid abroad while presenting an idealistic image of the United States during the Cold War.

questions.q: President Kennedy committed the nation in 1961 to what goal?
options: Building a permanent space station by the mid-1960s
Landing a man on the moon before the decade ended
Sending the first crewed mission to Mars by 1970
Launching the first satellite to orbit the moon
questions.explain: Kennedy's goal unified the Apollo program, which landed astronauts on the moon in July 1969.

questions.q: Who were the first two humans to walk on the moon during Apollo 11 in July 1969?
options: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin
John Glenn and Scott Carpenter
Frank Borman and Jim Lovell
Pete Conrad and Alan Bean
questions.explain: Armstrong and Aldrin landed in the lunar module while Michael Collins stayed in orbit in the command module.

questions.q: Who became the first American to orbit the Earth, in February 1962?
options: Alan Shepard
Neil Armstrong
John Glenn
Scott Carpenter
questions.explain: Glenn flew Friendship 7 for three orbits, answering the Soviet lead after Yuri Gagarin's flight in 1961.

questions.q: Which Soviet cosmonaut became the first human in space, in April 1961?
options: Alexei Leonov
Gherman Titov
Valentina Tereshkova
Yuri Gagarin
questions.explain: Gagarin's single orbit came less than a month before Alan Shepard's brief American suborbital flight.

questions.q: What happened to Apollo 1 in January 1967?
options: A fire during a launch rehearsal killed three astronauts
The capsule burned up during re-entry over the Pacific
The rocket exploded shortly after liftoff from Cape Kennedy
The crew was lost during a failed lunar orbit insertion
questions.explain: The fire killed Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee on the pad and led to a major redesign of the spacecraft.

questions.q: What was the outcome of the Apollo 13 mission in April 1970?
options: The crew landed on the moon but could not lift off for days
The mission was cancelled on the pad after a launch fire
An oxygen tank exploded but the crew returned safely to Earth
The crew was lost in deep space after a guidance failure
questions.explain: The explosion forced Americans to abandon a landing, and ground teams improvised ways to bring the astronauts home.

questions.q: The Apollo-Soyuz Test Project of 1975 was noteworthy because it did what?
options: Landed the first unmanned probe on the surface of Mars
Linked American and Soviet spacecraft in orbit
Placed the Hubble telescope in Earth orbit
Carried the first female astronauts into orbit together
questions.explain: The joint docking symbolized the easing of tensions in the era of detente.

questions.q: What was Skylab, launched by the United States in 1973?
options: A lunar rover used on Apollo missions
The first American space station
A communications satellite network
A reusable space shuttle prototype
questions.explain: Skylab hosted three crews in 1973 and 1974, studying long-term effects of space living and the sun.

questions.q: Which aircraft test pilot first flew faster than the speed of sound, in 1947?
options: Neil Armstrong
Gus Grissom
Francis Gary Powers
Chuck Yeager
questions.explain: Yeager flew the rocket-powered Bell X-1 in October 1947, an achievement during early Cold War aviation research.

questions.q: The Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum building on the National Mall opened in 1976 to mark what?
options: The Apollo 11 landing's tenth anniversary
The founding of NASA
The nation's bicentennial
The end of the Vietnam War
questions.explain: The museum opened on July 1, 1976, as part of the bicentennial celebrations and has displayed Apollo and Mercury craft.

questions.q: Why did the Space Race matter to American leaders during the Cold War?
options: Space achievements were seen as proof of technological and political strength
It was required under the terms of the Marshall Plan and the NATO treaty
It served as a means of settling border disputes with the Soviet Union
It replaced the need for nuclear weapons in American defense planning and budgets
questions.explain: Each Soviet and American success was treated as a measure of the rival systems, so the contest drew large federal spending.

questions.q: Which legislation of 1958 gave federal loans and grants to improve science, math, and foreign language education after Sputnik?
options: Elementary and Secondary Education Act
Higher Education Facilities Act
Vocational Education Act
National Defense Education Act
questions.explain: The law tied schooling to national security and expanded the federal role in education.

questions.q: The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, known as the GI Bill, offered veterans what?
options: Free land grants in the western territories and farm tools
Aid for education, home loans, and unemployment benefits
Automatic federal jobs with guaranteed promotion after discharge
Lifetime pensions after one year of military service
questions.explain: Millions of veterans used it for college and mortgages, which helped build the postwar middle class and suburbs.

questions.q: Which factor limited the benefits of the GI Bill for many Black veterans?
options: A provision in the law excluding Black veterans from benefits
A lack of interest in attending college among Black veterans
Discriminatory practices by banks, colleges, and local officials
Federal rules barring them from using benefits in the South
questions.explain: The law was written without a racial exclusion but was administered locally, and many Black veterans met discrimination in loans and admissions.

questions.q: What was the postwar trend known as the "baby boom"?
options: A sharp rise in the birth rate lasting from the mid-1940s to the early 1960s
A large migration of American families to Canada during the 1950s and 1960s
A surge in births concentrated among new immigrants from southern Europe
A steep decline in marriage rates and household formation after 1945
questions.explain: Births climbed after the war, crowding schools and boosting demand for housing and consumer goods.

questions.q: Levittown, built in Long Island in the late 1940s, is best known as what?
options: A mass-produced suburban housing development
A planned city built for wartime defense workers
A federal housing project for low-income families
A retirement community for aging veterans
questions.explain: William Levitt used assembly-line methods to build affordable homes, though deeds in his developments barred sales to Black families.

questions.q: What was redlining?
options: Setting a maximum interest rate that lenders could charge in minority neighborhoods
Denying loans or insurance in neighborhoods based on racial and ethnic composition
Giving tax breaks to buyers who purchased homes in new suburban developments
Marking highway routes in red to plan demolition of older city districts
questions.explain: Federal and private lenders marked minority areas as high-risk, which limited homeownership and contributed to segregation.

questions.q: Which development in the 1950s most encouraged suburban growth?
options: A decline in birth rates among young couples
A ban on new factories within city limits
The spread of automobiles and new highways
Rising prices for farmland near major cities
questions.explain: Cheaper cars, cheap gasoline, and new roads made commuting from suburbs practical for many middle-class families.

questions.q: What new medium brought entertainment and advertising into most American homes during the 1950s?
options: Cable satellites
Personal computers
Pocket radios
Television
questions.explain: Television sets spread from a small fraction of homes in 1950 to most households by the end of the decade.

questions.q: Which 1960 event is considered a turning point for television in politics?
options: The Army-McCarthy hearings
Eisenhower's farewell
The Checkers speech
The Kennedy-Nixon debates
questions.explain: The first televised general-election presidential debates drew a huge audience, and many believed Kennedy's appearance helped him.

questions.q: The 22nd Amendment, ratified in 1951, did what?
options: Limited presidents to two elected terms
Lowered the voting age to 18 in federal elections
Replaced the Electoral College with a direct vote
Allowed direct election of senators
questions.explain: The amendment followed Franklin Roosevelt's four elections and exempted the sitting president, Harry Truman.

questions.q: The 23rd Amendment, ratified in 1961, did what for the nation's capital?
options: Made the District of Columbia a state with two senators
Gave residents of Washington electors in presidential elections
Created an elected mayor and city council for Washington
Gave the District full voting members in both houses of Congress
questions.explain: Residents of the District had no presidential vote before the amendment, which gave it as many electors as it would have as a state, but no more than the least populous state.

questions.q: What did the District of Columbia Home Rule Act of 1973 create?
options: Statehood for the District with two voting senators
A new federal capital built outside the city
An elected mayor and city council for the District
Full voting seats in both houses of Congress
questions.explain: Congress kept authority to review local laws, but residents gained the right to choose their local government.

questions.q: Which law of 1947 reorganized the military and created the CIA and the National Security Council?
options: The Taft-Hartley Labor Act
The Neutrality Act of 1939
The Lend-Lease Act of 1941
The National Security Act
questions.explain: The act unified the services under a new department and set up a framework for managing Cold War intelligence and strategy.

questions.q: Why did the Taft-Hartley Act of 1947 anger organized labor?
options: It abolished the federal minimum wage and overtime protections for workers
It required all workers in covered industries to join unions at once
It restricted union practices such as closed shops and certain strikes
It outlawed collective bargaining in all private industries nationwide
questions.explain: Congress passed it over Truman's veto, and unions called it a "slave labor" law.

questions.q: Which result of the 1948 presidential election was a famous surprise?
options: Truman's defeat of Thomas Dewey
Eisenhower's defeat of Stevenson
Kennedy's defeat of Nixon
Johnson's defeat of Goldwater
questions.explain: Polls and newspapers predicted a Dewey win, but Truman won after a vigorous campaign against a "do-nothing" Congress.

questions.q: The States' Rights Democratic Party, or Dixiecrats, ran Strom Thurmond in 1948 largely because of what?
options: Opposition to the Marshall Plan and the Truman Doctrine
Opposition to the Democratic civil rights platform
Anger over Truman's peacetime military draft proposal
A dispute over the Taft-Hartley veto and union policy
questions.explain: Southern delegates walked out when the convention endorsed a stronger civil rights plank.

questions.q: At the end of World War II the United States occupied Japan under which general?
options: George Marshall
Dwight Eisenhower
Douglas MacArthur
Omar Bradley
questions.explain: MacArthur led the occupation, which promoted a new constitution in 1947 and democratic reforms.

questions.q: The Nuremberg trials of 1945 and 1946 prosecuted what?
options: Nazi leaders for war crimes and crimes against humanity
Japanese military officers for wartime atrocities in Asia
Soviet leaders for violating wartime treaty obligations
Allied commanders for the bombing of German cities
questions.explain: An international tribunal tried top Nazi officials, setting precedents in international law.

questions.q: The Bretton Woods conference of 1944 created which two institutions?
options: The United Nations and the Marshall Plan agency
The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank
The Federal Reserve and the Treasury Department
The World Trade Organization and the World Bank
questions.explain: Allied delegates built a postwar economic order with the dollar tied to gold and other currencies pegged to the dollar.

questions.q: The United Nations was founded in 1945 mainly to do what?
options: Rebuild the economies of postwar Europe
Enforce binding rules on international trade
Administer the occupied zones of Germany and Japan
Maintain international peace and security
questions.explain: Fifty nations signed the charter in San Francisco, creating a Security Council with five permanent members that hold a veto.

questions.q: The Marshall Plan was named for which official?
options: Secretary of Defense James Forrestal
Secretary of State George C. Marshall
Under Secretary of State Dean Acheson
Treasury Secretary John W. Snyder
questions.explain: Marshall announced the plan in a 1947 Harvard speech, and the program won him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1953.

questions.q: Which wartime conference of 1945 left Germany divided into occupation zones under the Allies?
options: Munich
Geneva
Potsdam
Versailles
questions.explain: The Allied leaders met in July 1945, setting up zones of occupation that later hardened into East and West Germany.

questions.q: In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), the Supreme Court ruled what about segregated public schools?
options: They were inherently unequal and unconstitutional
They were legal as long as facilities were roughly equal
They could remain segregated in the Southern states only
They were a matter for each state legislature to decide
questions.explain: The unanimous decision, written by Chief Justice Earl Warren, rejected the separate-but-equal doctrine in public education.

questions.q: Which earlier Supreme Court decision did Brown v. Board of Education effectively overturn in the field of education?
options: Dred Scott v. Sandford
Korematsu v. United States
Lochner v. New York
Plessy v. Ferguson
questions.explain: Plessy in 1896 had approved separate-but-equal facilities; Brown held that separate schooling was unequal.

questions.q: The 1955 follow-up ruling known as Brown II ordered schools to desegregate with what pace?
options: "Within one calendar year"
"With all deliberate speed"
"Before the 1956 election"
"Only with local approval"
questions.explain: The vague phrase gave local officials room to delay, and many Southern districts resisted for years.

questions.q: What event in 1955 helped draw national attention to racial violence in Mississippi?
options: The bombing of a Birmingham church
The shooting of NAACP leader Medgar Evers
The lynching of Mack Charles Parker
The murder of 14-year-old Emmett Till
questions.explain: Till's mother insisted on an open casket funeral in Chicago, and photographs spread widely in the Black press.

questions.q: Which action by Rosa Parks in December 1955 helped spark the Montgomery bus boycott?
options: Refusing to yield her bus seat to a white rider
Leading a sit-in at a department store lunch counter
Registering to vote at the county courthouse
Speaking at a mass rally at a Baptist church
questions.explain: Her arrest led local activists to organize a boycott of the city's buses that lasted more than a year.

questions.q: The Montgomery bus boycott brought which young minister to national prominence?
options: Rev. Jesse L. Jackson
Ralph David Abernathy
Martin Luther King Jr.
Andrew J. Young Jr.
questions.explain: Chosen to lead the Montgomery Improvement Association, King became a national voice for nonviolent protest.

questions.q: How did the Montgomery bus boycott finally succeed?
options: Congress passed a law banning segregation on all interstate buses in 1957
The city commission voted to end bus segregation after talks with boycott leaders
The bus company went bankrupt after losing most of its Black riders
The Supreme Court affirmed that bus segregation was unconstitutional
questions.explain: After the Court affirmed Browder v. Gayle in late 1956, Montgomery's buses were integrated after a boycott of about 381 days.

questions.q: The Southern Christian Leadership Conference, founded in 1957, was built mainly on what foundation?
options: Labor unions and mass strikes in industry
Black churches and nonviolent direct action
Federal agencies and court-ordered programs
Northern college campuses and student groups
questions.explain: SCLC, with King as president, coordinated church-based protests across the South.

questions.q: What was the principle of nonviolent resistance, as practiced by King, meant to do?
options: Expose injustice and win public sympathy without force
Avoid all contact with officials and local authorities
Raise money for lawsuits and legal defense funds
Prevent arrests by avoiding public demonstrations
questions.explain: King drew on Christian teaching and Gandhi to argue that peaceful suffering could shame opponents and move public opinion.

questions.q: At Little Rock in 1957, what did President Eisenhower do when Governor Orval Faubus used the National Guard to block nine Black students from Central High?
options: He allowed the school to close for the year
He asked the NAACP to delay the students' entry
He sent federal troops to protect the students
He accepted Faubus's plan to phase in one student a year
questions.explain: The 101st Airborne Division escorted the students, a rare use of federal troops to enforce a court order for desegregation.

questions.q: The Supreme Court case Cooper v. Aaron (1958) reinforced what principle after the Little Rock crisis?
options: States may nullify federal court rulings within their borders
States must obey the Court's interpretation of the Constitution
Schools may close temporarily to avoid court-ordered integration
Private academies must integrate if they receive state funds
questions.explain: The justices rejected Arkansas officials' claim that they could ignore Brown and affirmed the Court's authority.

questions.q: Which 1960 protest by four college students at a Woolworth lunch counter sparked a wave of sit-ins?
options: Greensboro, North Carolina
Chattanooga, Tennessee
Little Rock, Arkansas
Charleston, South Carolina
questions.explain: The Greensboro sit-in on February 1, 1960, spread to dozens of cities, and part of that counter is displayed at the Smithsonian.

questions.q: Where can visitors see a section of the Greensboro lunch counter in Washington?
options: The National Archives Building on Constitution Avenue
The Library of Congress's Jefferson Building exhibit hall
The National Gallery of Art on the National Mall
The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History
questions.explain: The counter from the Woolworth store was acquired by the Smithsonian and became part of its American history collections.

questions.q: The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) was formed in 1960 to do what?
options: Replace the NAACP's legal strategy in the courts
Organize an armed defense force in the South
Give young activists a role in the movement
Run candidates for Congress in Southern districts
questions.explain: Young sit-in participants formed SNCC with advice from Ella Baker, favoring grassroots organizing over top-down leadership.

questions.q: What was the goal of the 1961 Freedom Rides, organized by CORE?
options: To test enforcement of bans on segregation in interstate buses
To raise money for voter registration drives in Mississippi
To protest segregation in the armed forces and military bases
To integrate Southern public universities by enrolling students
questions.explain: Riders sat together on buses and in terminals through the South and met violence, but the federal government then enforced the ban.

questions.q: Which 1963 campaign in Alabama used marches, fire hoses, and police dogs seen on television?
options: The Selma voting rights march
The Albany Georgia protests
The Freedom Summer project
The Birmingham campaign
questions.explain: Public Safety Commissioner Bull Connor's harsh response in Birmingham shocked viewers and strengthened support for federal civil rights legislation.

questions.q: King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail" was written in response to what?
options: An injunction from a state judge banning further marches
A request from Birmingham's mayor that he leave the city
A statement by white clergy who criticized the protests as untimely
A newspaper editorial by Birmingham's mayor condemning the boycott
questions.explain: King defended nonviolent direct action and argued that people have a moral duty to resist unjust laws.

questions.q: In a televised speech in June 1963, what did President Kennedy call civil rights?
options: A question for the states to settle
A moral issue as old as the Scriptures
A passing concern of party politics
A problem for the federal courts
questions.explain: Kennedy announced he would send Congress a civil rights bill, which became the basis for the 1964 law.

questions.q: Where did the 1963 March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom reach its climax?
options: On the Capitol steps
At the Lincoln Memorial
At the White House gates
At the Supreme Court plaza
questions.explain: Marchers gathered at the Washington Monument and walked to the Lincoln Memorial, where speakers addressed a crowd of roughly 250,000.

questions.q: On what date was the March on Washington held?
options: August 28, 1963
August 28, 1964
October 2, 1963
questions.explain: The march took place on a late-summer day in 1963, months before the Civil Rights Act was passed.

questions.q: Which two leaders were the main organizers of the March on Washington?
options: Malcolm X and Stokely Carmichael
Thurgood Marshall and Roy Wilkins
James Farmer and Ralph Abernathy
Asa Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin
questions.explain: Randolph, a labor leader, proposed the march and Rustin handled the detailed planning.

questions.q: What were the March on Washington's official demands?
options: A separate Black homeland in the Deep South and reparations
Immediate withdrawal of troops from Vietnam and cuts in defense
Civil rights legislation, jobs, and a higher minimum wage
A constitutional convention and abolition of the Senate
questions.explain: The march's name linked economic opportunity to equal rights, and its demands included a federal jobs program and an end to segregation.

questions.q: In which speech at the Lincoln Memorial did Martin Luther King Jr. describe a dream of racial equality?
options: "Beyond Vietnam"
"I Have a Dream"
"Why We Can't Wait"
"A Time for Choosing"
questions.explain: King's address ended the day's program and linked the promises of the Declaration of Independence to the unfinished work of civil rights.

questions.q: King began the "I Have a Dream" speech by invoking which earlier document?
options: The Articles of Confederation
The Northwest Ordinance of 1787
The Bill of Rights of 1791
The Emancipation Proclamation
questions.explain: He opened with the reference to "five score years ago," recalling Abraham Lincoln, in whose memorial the speech was delivered.

questions.q: In the "I Have a Dream" speech, King described the promise of the Constitution and the Declaration of Independence as what?
options: A treaty guaranteeing peace between the North and South
A binding legal contract among the original thirteen states
A promissory note to which every American was to fall heir
A solemn pledge of peace made to other nations
questions.explain: He used the image of a bad check to say the nation had not honored its promise of equality to Black citizens.

questions.q: Which young leader of SNCC was the youngest speaker at the 1963 March on Washington?
options: John Lewis
Julian Bond
Bob Moses
James Forman
questions.explain: Lewis, later a congressman, gave a forceful speech, and march leaders asked him to tone down parts of the text.

questions.q: Which musical artists performed at the 1963 March on Washington?
options: Elvis Presley and Pat Boone
The Beach Boys and Chuck Berry
Mahalia Jackson and Joan Baez
Frank Sinatra and Ella Fitzgerald
questions.explain: Gospel and folk singers performed, including Jackson, Baez, Bob Dylan, and Peter, Paul and Mary.

questions.q: How did President Kennedy meet with march leaders on the day of the March on Washington?
options: He addressed the crowd at the Lincoln Memorial
He declined to meet them and watched from the Oval Office
He was traveling abroad on a state visit that week
He received them at the White House after the event
questions.explain: Leaders met with the president after the march, and the peaceful event helped build momentum for a civil rights bill.

questions.q: The 1957 Prayer Pilgrimage for Freedom, where King spoke on voting rights, was held at which place?
options: The Lincoln Memorial
The Jefferson Memorial
The Washington Monument
The Capitol Rotunda
questions.explain: King gave his first major national address there on the third anniversary of Brown, urging Americans to give Black citizens the ballot.

questions.q: The Poor People's Campaign of 1968 set up a shanty encampment near the Lincoln Memorial called what?
options: Freedom Village
Resurrection City
Solidarity Village
Unity Encampment
questions.explain: The campaign continued King's plans to press for economic justice, and thousands lived in the camp in May and June 1968.

questions.q: What event on September 15, 1963, intensified national outrage soon after the March on Washington?
options: The shooting of NAACP field secretary Medgar Evers in Jackson
The assassination of President Kennedy in Dallas, Texas
A bombing at a Birmingham church that killed four girls
The Watts riot in Los Angeles that left dozens dead
questions.explain: The bombing of the 16th Street Baptist Church shocked the nation and added pressure on Congress.

questions.q: What parliamentary tactic did Southern senators use against the Civil Rights Act of 1964?
options: A presidential veto
A Senate filibuster
A vote of censure
A recess appointment
questions.explain: Senators led by Richard Russell held the floor to block the bill, and it passed only after the Senate voted for cloture.

questions.q: What level of support did the Senate's cloture rule require in 1964 to end debate?
options: A simple majority of senators
Unanimous consent from senators
Three-fifths of the whole Senate
Two-thirds of those voting
questions.explain: In 1964 Rule 22 required two-thirds of senators present and voting; the Senate voted 71 to 29 for cloture, with help from Republican Everett Dirksen.

questions.q: Which title of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned discrimination in hotels, restaurants, and theaters?
options: Title II
Title VII
Title IV
Title IX
questions.explain: Title II prohibited racial discrimination in public accommodations; employment discrimination was covered in Title VII.

questions.q: Which part of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned discrimination in employment and created the EEOC?
options: Title II
Title VIII
Title VII
Title VI
questions.explain: The act barred job bias based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin and established the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

questions.q: Which President signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 into law?
options: Lyndon B. Johnson
John F. Kennedy
Richard M. Nixon
Dwight D. Eisenhower
questions.explain: Johnson signed it on July 2, 1964, saying that the law should end racial divisions, and he had pushed it as a memorial to Kennedy.

questions.q: In Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States (1964), the Supreme Court upheld the Civil Rights Act's public accommodations section using which power of Congress?
options: The power to tax and spend for welfare
The power to establish post offices
The power to set naturalization rules
The power to regulate interstate commerce
questions.explain: The Court held that segregation in motels could burden travel across state lines, so Congress could regulate it under the Commerce Clause.

questions.q: The 24th Amendment, ratified in 1964, did what?
options: Lowered the voting age to 18 nationwide
Banned poll taxes in federal elections
Limited presidents to two terms in office
Created a national voter registration list
questions.explain: Poll taxes had been used in several Southern states to keep poor and Black citizens from voting.

questions.q: What was the Freedom Summer of 1964?
options: A national bus tour of Northern cities by civil rights leaders
A march from Selma to Montgomery to demand voting rights
A boycott of Southern department stores by Black shoppers
A Mississippi voter registration drive run by civil rights groups
questions.explain: Hundreds of volunteers, many of them northern students, taught in Freedom Schools and tried to register Black voters.

questions.q: What was the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party in 1964?
options: An integrated party challenging the all-white state delegation at the convention
A Black separatist party that sought its own state within the Deep South
A branch of the Republican Party that backed Barry Goldwater in the state
A labor union for Mississippi sharecroppers and cotton field workers
questions.explain: It argued that the regular delegation did not represent Mississippi's population, and it was offered only two seats.

questions.q: Which 1965 march in Alabama, attacked by state troopers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge, built support for voting rights?
options: The Birmingham children's march
The Selma to Montgomery march
The Mississippi March Against Fear
The Albany Movement marches
questions.explain: Televised images of "Bloody Sunday" on March 7, 1965, led President Johnson to call for a strong voting rights law.

questions.q: President Johnson called for the Voting Rights Act in a televised address to Congress that used which phrase from the movement?
options: "Black is beautiful"
"Freedom in our time"
"We shall overcome"
"Eyes on the prize"
questions.explain: Johnson used the song's title to show that he stood with the demonstrators, within days of the violence in Selma.

questions.q: What did the Voting Rights Act of 1965 do?
options: Guaranteed women the right to vote and ended property requirements
Lowered the voting age to 18 and required automatic registration
Abolished the Electoral College and required direct election of presidents
Banned literacy tests and allowed federal oversight of voter registration
questions.explain: The law targeted barriers used to keep Black citizens from voting and brought a large rise in Black registration in the South.

questions.q: What was Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act?
options: It banned the secret ballot in federal elections to deter fraud
It required covered areas to get federal approval for voting changes
It outlawed all party primaries and required general elections only
It lowered the voting age to 18 in all federal elections
questions.explain: The preclearance rule covered jurisdictions with a history of discrimination and was a major enforcement tool.

questions.q: In Shelby County v. Holder (2013), the Supreme Court did what?
options: Struck down the formula that decided which areas needed preclearance
Banned literacy tests nationwide in all federal elections
Declared the Voting Rights Act unconstitutional in its entirety
Created a national photo voter ID requirement for elections
questions.explain: The 5-4 ruling left Section 5 in place but said the coverage formula was outdated, so it could not be enforced until Congress adopted a new one.

questions.q: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 is often described as enforcing the guarantee of which amendment?
options: The 13th Amendment
The 19th Amendment
The 15th Amendment
The 26th Amendment
questions.explain: The 15th Amendment barred denial of the vote based on race, and the 1965 law gave Congress and the courts new ways to enforce it.

questions.q: Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections (1966) held what about poll taxes?
options: They were valid in all state and local races
They were allowed only for local offices
They were unconstitutional in state elections
They were valid if set below five dollars a year
questions.explain: The Court said wealth or fee payment could not be a condition for voting under the Equal Protection Clause.

questions.q: Loving v. Virginia (1967) struck down laws that banned what?
options: Public school prayer
Interracial marriage
Racial job quotas
Segregated public parks
questions.explain: The unanimous Court held that Virginia's ban violated the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses.

questions.q: Malcolm X left which organization in 1964 before he was assassinated in February 1965?
options: The Nation of Islam
The Urban League
The Deacons for Defense
The Black Panther Party
questions.explain: After a pilgrimage to Mecca, he softened his views on race and founded his own groups before being shot in New York.

questions.q: What did the slogan "Black Power," popularized by Stokely Carmichael in 1966, emphasize?
options: Federal government control of all Black public schools
Emigration of Black Americans to Africa or the Caribbean
Strict nonviolence and full integration into white institutions
Black pride, self-determination, and political and economic strength
questions.explain: The slogan reflected frustration with the pace of change and led to debates inside the movement about nonviolence and integration.

questions.q: The Black Panther Party, founded in 1966 in Oakland, California, by Huey Newton and Bobby Seale, began by doing what?
options: Running voter registration drives in rural Mississippi towns
Organizing bus boycotts and sit-ins in California cities
Lobbying Congress for a federal full-employment act
Patrolling police activity and then running community programs
questions.explain: The party carried weapons at first but also ran free breakfast programs and health clinics.

questions.q: The riot in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles in August 1965 showed what?
options: Widespread opposition to the escalating war in Vietnam
The growing influence of unions among Black workers in Los Angeles
Frustration over poverty and discrimination outside the South
A backlash against passage of the Voting Rights Act in Congress
questions.explain: Days of unrest after a traffic stop left dozens dead and revealed problems of segregation and joblessness in Northern cities.

questions.q: The Kerner Commission of 1968 concluded that the nation was moving toward what?
options: Two societies, one Black and one white, separate and unequal
A new era of racial equality and economic integration
A return to Jim Crow segregation laws across the nation
A permanent split between rural America and the cities
questions.explain: President Johnson's commission blamed white racism, segregation, and poverty for the riots of the mid-1960s.

questions.q: In his 1967 speech "Beyond Vietnam," King argued that what?
options: The war would end soon if troop levels were doubled
The war diverted resources from the poor and was morally wrong
The war was necessary to stop communism and should be escalated
Congress should formally declare war on North Vietnam
questions.explain: King broke with the Johnson administration and linked the war abroad to injustice at home, drawing criticism from some allies.

questions.q: Where was Martin Luther King Jr. assassinated on April 4, 1968?
options: Atlanta, Georgia
Washington, D.C.
Montgomery, Alabama
Memphis, Tennessee
questions.explain: King was in Memphis to support striking sanitation workers when he was shot on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel.

questions.q: What national reaction followed King's assassination?
options: Riots in many cities, including Washington
A nationwide general strike by labor unions
Immediate repeal of all segregation laws in Tennessee
A one-year pause in all presidential campaigning
questions.explain: Grief and anger set off unrest in more than a hundred cities, and parts of Washington were burned.

questions.q: Which law, signed a week after King's death, banned discrimination in the sale and rental of housing?
options: The Civil Rights Act of 1964
The Fair Housing Act of 1968
The Housing Act of 1949
The Voting Rights Act of 1965
questions.explain: Part of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, it was passed after King's death and enforced by the Department of Housing and Urban Development.

questions.q: Which federal holiday honors Martin Luther King Jr. each January?
options: Martin Luther King Jr. Day
Juneteenth Independence Day
Presidents' Day holiday
Veterans Day observance
questions.explain: President Reagan signed the holiday into law in 1983, and it was first observed as a federal holiday in 1986 on the third Monday of January; every state observed it by 2000.

questions.q: The King Memorial lies between which two memorials, aligned in a line of sight?
options: The Washington Monument and the Capitol
The Vietnam and Korean memorials
The WWII and Korean War memorials
The Lincoln and Jefferson memorials
questions.explain: Placed on the Tidal Basin's edge, the King Memorial sits near the Lincoln and Jefferson memorials, linking the legacy of the Declaration and emancipation.

questions.q: Which prize did King win in 1964?
options: The Pulitzer Prize
The Nobel Peace Prize
The Gandhi Peace Prize
The Templeton Prize
questions.explain: At 35 he was the youngest person to receive the Peace Prize at that time, and he donated the prize money to the movement.

questions.q: The National Museum of African American History and Culture opened on the National Mall in what year?
questions.explain: Congress created it in 2003, and it opened in September 2016 as a Smithsonian museum focusing on Black American life.

questions.q: Affirmative action in federal contracting began with which action by President Johnson in 1965?
options: Executive Order 11246
Executive Order 10925
Executive Order 8802
Executive Order 9981
questions.explain: The order required federal contractors to take steps to ensure equal opportunity and was later expanded to cover sex.

questions.q: The Supreme Court's 1978 decision in Regents of the University of California v. Bakke ruled what?
options: Fixed racial quotas were unconstitutional, but race could be one factor
Race could never be considered in admissions decisions of any kind
Colleges could use fixed quotas to remedy past societal discrimination
Private colleges had to admit applicants strictly by test scores
questions.explain: The divided Court struck down the medical school's set-aside seats but allowed using race to promote diversity.

questions.q: In Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg (1971), the Supreme Court approved which method to desegregate schools?
options: Closing public schools
Voluntary transfers only
Court-ordered busing
Building new schools
questions.explain: Because neighborhoods were segregated, the Court allowed judges to order busing, and the policy provoked protests in many cities.

questions.q: In Milliken v. Bradley (1974), the Supreme Court limited desegregation by ruling what?
options: Busing to achieve integration was unconstitutional in all cases
Schools had no duty to integrate even after proven intentional bias
Courts could merge city and suburban districts into one unified system
Courts generally could not order busing across city-suburb district lines
questions.explain: The Court held that suburbs were not to be included absent proof of their own discrimination, which left many city schools segregated.

questions.q: In Griggs v. Duke Power Co. (1971), the Supreme Court held that employers' tests and requirements were illegal if they did what?
options: Were written by outside consultants rather than company staff
Had a discriminatory effect and were not related to job performance
Were given at times inconvenient for working applicants
Were used for hiring but not for promotions inside the firm
questions.explain: The decision recognized disparate impact under Title VII of the 1964 Civil Rights Act.

questions.q: Which 1948 decision held that courts could not enforce racially restrictive housing covenants?
options: Shelley v. Kraemer
Sweatt v. Painter
Mendez v. Westminster
Hernandez v. Texas
questions.explain: The Court held that judicial enforcement of such covenants amounted to state action that violated the 14th Amendment.

questions.q: Who broke baseball's color line in 1947 when he joined the Brooklyn Dodgers?
options: Satchel Paige
Jackie Robinson
Monte Irvin
Roy Campanella
questions.explain: Robinson's debut broke the major leagues' modern color line, years before most schools were desegregated.

questions.q: Who was the lead attorney for the NAACP in Brown v. Board of Education and later became a Supreme Court justice?
options: Jack Greenberg
Robert L. Carter
Thurgood Marshall
Spottswood Robinson
questions.explain: Marshall argued the case in December 1952 and again in December 1953, and President Johnson appointed him to the Court in 1967, the first Black justice.

questions.q: Which president appointed Thurgood Marshall to the Supreme Court in 1967?
options: John Kennedy
Richard Nixon
Harry Truman
Lyndon Johnson
questions.explain: Johnson's appointment made Marshall the first African American justice, and he served until 1991.

questions.q: Which Black member of Congress became the first Black woman to seek a major party's presidential nomination, in 1972?
options: Barbara Jordan
Shirley Chisholm
Carol Moseley Braun
Eleanor Holmes Norton
questions.explain: Chisholm was elected to the House in 1968 and ran in the Democratic primaries in 1972.

questions.q: The Civil Rights Act of 1957 was notable for what reason?
options: It ended segregation in public schools across the South
It banned poll taxes in federal and state elections nationwide
It was the first federal civil rights law since Reconstruction
It made lynching a federal crime punishable by death
questions.explain: Though weak in enforcement, it created the Civil Rights Division of the Justice Department and the Civil Rights Commission.

questions.q: The 1956 "Southern Manifesto" signed by many Southern members of Congress did what?
options: Denounced Brown v. Board and urged resistance to it
Endorsed the Montgomery bus boycott as lawful protest
Supported a constitutional ban on poll taxes nationwide
Called for a convention to rewrite the Constitution
questions.explain: About a hundred lawmakers called the ruling an abuse of judicial power, a sign of organized resistance to integration.

questions.q: Which labor leader first proposed a March on Washington in 1941, forcing Roosevelt to act on defense industry jobs?
options: Walter P. Reuther
Joseph A. Beirne
David Dubinsky
Asa Philip Randolph
questions.explain: Randolph called off the 1941 march after Executive Order 8802 banned discrimination in defense industries, and he returned to the idea in 1963.

questions.q: Which woman, a longtime organizer, helped found SNCC and urged group-centered leadership?
options: Daisy Bates
Septima Clark
Dorothy Height
Ella Baker
questions.explain: Baker advised students in 1960 to build their own organization rather than become the youth wing of SCLC.

questions.q: Fannie Lou Hamer became nationally known in 1964 for what?
options: Leading the first march across the Edmund Pettus Bridge
Testifying to the Democratic convention about voter-drive violence
Founding the Southern Christian Leadership Conference
Winning a Supreme Court case against Mississippi voting laws
questions.explain: Her televised testimony about being beaten after trying to register moved viewers and drew attention to Mississippi's exclusion of Black voters.

questions.q: What was the effect of the Voting Rights Act on elected Black officials in the South?
options: The number rose sharply in the years after its passage
The number fell as white backlash grew in the Deep South
There was little change in Black officeholding for decades
Black candidates were barred from running for state office
questions.explain: As more Black citizens registered, they began winning local, state, and federal offices that had been closed to them.

questions.q: Which ruling in 1960, Boynton v. Virginia, was tested by the Freedom Riders?
options: Segregated public parks were legal if they were equal
Bans on interracial marriage were constitutional
Segregation in interstate bus terminals was illegal
Private lunch counters had to integrate nationwide
questions.explain: The Court's decision was not enforced in much of the South, so the Freedom Riders tested whether it would be.

questions.q: The 1954 Geneva Accords ended French rule in Indochina and temporarily divided Vietnam at which line?
options: The 17th parallel
The 38th parallel
The Mekong River
The Red River line
questions.explain: The agreement set a military line and called for nationwide elections in 1956, which South Vietnam's government and the United States did not support.

questions.q: Which French defeat in 1954 ended France's attempt to keep control of Vietnam?
options: Hue Citadel
Khe Sanh Base
Ia Drang Valley
Dien Bien Phu
questions.explain: Vietnamese forces led by Ho Chi Minh besieged and captured the French base, and France then agreed to withdraw.

questions.q: The United States supported the government of which South Vietnamese leader in the late 1950s and early 1960s?
options: Nguyen Van Thieu
Ngo Dinh Diem
Nguyen Cao Ky
Duong Van Minh
questions.explain: Diem was seen as an anti-communist, but his repression of Buddhists lost him support, and he was overthrown and killed in 1963.

questions.q: What was the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution of 1964?
options: A UN resolution calling for a cease-fire and talks between the two Vietnams
A treaty with North Vietnam that set terms for American troop withdrawals
A measure authorizing the president to use military force in Southeast Asia
A law that created the draft lottery and ended most student deferments
questions.explain: After reports of attacks on American destroyers, Congress gave Lyndon Johnson wide authority to respond, and he used it to expand the war.

questions.q: How did Congress vote on the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution in August 1964?
options: Narrowly, along party lines, with most Republicans opposed
It failed in the Senate but passed the House overwhelmingly
It passed the House only, as the Senate never voted on it
Nearly unanimously, with only two Senate votes against
questions.explain: The House approved it unanimously and the Senate by 88 to 2, with Wayne Morse and Ernest Gruening opposed.

questions.q: Which senators cast the only two votes against the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution?
options: William Fulbright and Mike Mansfield
Barry Goldwater and Strom Thurmond
Wayne Morse and Ernest Gruening
Robert Kennedy and Eugene McCarthy
questions.explain: Both opposed giving the president a blank check, and Morse warned it would lead to a major war.

questions.q: Which bombing campaign, begun in 1965, aimed to pressure North Vietnam by sustained air attacks?
options: Operation Desert Storm
Operation Rolling Thunder
Operation Market Garden
Operation Linebacker II
questions.explain: The campaign lasted until 1968, but it did not stop supplies reaching communist forces in the South.

questions.q: What happened in March 1965 that marked a turning point in American involvement in Vietnam?
options: The first U.S. combat Marines landed at Da Nang
The Paris peace talks between the U.S. and Hanoi began
The draft ended and the army became all-volunteer
President Johnson made a wartime visit to Saigon
questions.explain: The landing of Marines, followed by larger deployments, changed the American role from advising to fighting.

questions.q: At the war's height in 1968 and 1969 about how many American troops were in Vietnam?
options: About 50,000
About 100,000
About 250,000
questions.explain: Troop levels peaked above 540,000 in 1969, and the draft was a main source of manpower.

questions.q: What was a common criticism of the Vietnam-era draft system?
options: The draft applied only to Black and Hispanic men, who were sent to combat in large numbers
Women were required to register and were drafted into combat support roles
It was paid for by a special war tax that fell mostly on college graduates
Critics said deferments let many middle-class men avoid service while poorer men were drafted
questions.explain: Critics said the deferment system favored the better-off, and that resentment helped lead to the lottery of 1969.

questions.q: The draft lottery that began in December 1969 selected young men by what method?
options: Birthdate drawing
Aptitude test scores
Home state quotas
Lists of volunteers
questions.explain: Capsules with birth dates were drawn to set the order of induction, which replaced the system run by local boards.

questions.q: The Viet Cong was the name for which group?
options: Regular South Vietnamese soldiers trained by the U.S.
Communist guerrillas fighting in South Vietnam
Chinese military advisers sent to North Vietnam
French Foreign Legion units that stayed after 1954
questions.explain: Backed by North Vietnam, the National Liberation Front used guerrilla tactics and tunnels against American and South Vietnamese forces.

questions.q: The Ho Chi Minh Trail was important because it was what?
options: A network of routes that carried supplies from North to South Vietnam
A highway built by the French to link Hanoi with Saigon along the coast
A fortified border zone along the 17th parallel dividing the two Vietnams
A path used by U.S. Marines to move troops from the coast inland
questions.explain: The trail ran through Laos and Cambodia, and American bombing there failed to cut it off.

questions.q: What was Agent Orange?
options: A code name for a secret bombing mission over Laos in 1969
A South Vietnamese political party that opposed Ngo Dinh Diem
A nerve gas used by North Vietnamese forces at Khe Sanh
A herbicide sprayed to clear forests and crops in Vietnam
questions.explain: The U.S. military used it to strip jungle cover, and later veterans and Vietnamese citizens reported serious health effects.

questions.q: The Tet Offensive of January 1968 was what?
options: A U.S. invasion of North Vietnam aimed at Hanoi and Haiphong
A coordinated communist attack on cities across South Vietnam
A peace agreement between Washington and Hanoi that ended the fighting
A U.S. bombing campaign against Hanoi and Haiphong harbor
questions.explain: Though the attackers suffered heavy losses, the scale surprised Americans who had been told the war was being won.

questions.q: How did the Tet Offensive affect American opinion?
options: It rallied nearly all Americans behind the war and its military leaders
It ended the antiwar movement because the offensive was defeated
It increased doubts about officials' optimism and the war's progress
It led Congress to pass a formal declaration of war on North Vietnam
questions.explain: Reports by journalists and the "credibility gap" led many to question whether the war could be won.

questions.q: What did President Johnson announce on March 31, 1968?
options: He would send 200,000 more troops
He would order troops into Laos
He would not seek reelection
He would end the war at once
questions.explain: Johnson also limited the bombing of North Vietnam and called for peace talks.

questions.q: What was the My Lai massacre of March 1968?
options: A North Vietnamese assault on the U.S. embassy compound in Saigon
An American bombing of Hanoi that destroyed civilian neighborhoods
A battle at the Cambodian border that cost many American lives
The killing of hundreds of Vietnamese civilians by American soldiers
questions.explain: News of the killing in 1969 deepened opposition to the war, and Lieutenant William Calley was later convicted.

questions.q: President Nixon's policy called Vietnamization sought to do what?
options: Increase American combat troops to force a quick military victory
Turn the ground fighting over to South Vietnam as U.S. troops withdrew
Divide Vietnam into three regions under joint American and Soviet control
Hand control of Vietnam to the UN and end all U.S. involvement
questions.explain: The plan aimed to withdraw gradually while keeping a non-communist government in Saigon.

questions.q: What was the "silent majority" in Nixon's 1969 speech?
options: Americans who he said quietly supported his Vietnam policy
Veterans who opposed the war but avoided public protest
Voters who stayed home from the polls in the 1968 election
Members of Congress who quietly voted against the war
questions.explain: Nixon appealed to those not joining protests, asking for patience as troops were withdrawn.

questions.q: Why did Nixon's April 1970 announcement of an invasion of Cambodia cause protests?
options: It violated a Supreme Court order limiting wartime operations
It appeared to widen a war he had promised to wind down
It broke the terms of the Geneva Accords signed in 1954
It ended draft deferments for college students that year
questions.explain: The action sparked demonstrations at campuses across the country, including Kent State.

questions.q: What happened at Kent State University on May 4, 1970?
options: Students occupied the administration building and held it for a week
Protesters burned the campus draft board office to the ground
A bomb exploded in the ROTC building, injuring dozens of students
National Guardsmen fired on antiwar protesters, killing four students
questions.explain: The shootings led to a nationwide student strike and hardened opinions on both sides.

questions.q: The 26th Amendment, ratified in 1971, did what?
options: Abolished poll taxes in elections
Gave Washington D.C. electoral votes
Lowered the voting age to 18
Limited presidents to two terms
questions.explain: Supporters said that those old enough to be drafted should be able to vote.

questions.q: What were the Pentagon Papers?
options: A secret Defense Department study of U.S. decision-making in Vietnam
Architectural plans for building the Pentagon during World War II
A report on the Cuban Missile Crisis prepared for President Kennedy
Secret minutes of NATO meetings on the defense of Western Europe
questions.explain: Ordered by Secretary Robert McNamara, the study of the war's history was leaked in 1971 by Daniel Ellsberg.

questions.q: Who leaked the Pentagon Papers to the press in 1971?
options: Bob Woodward
Seymour Hersh
Daniel Ellsberg
Walter Cronkite
questions.explain: Ellsberg, a former Defense Department analyst, copied the study and gave it to newspapers including the New York Times.

questions.q: In New York Times Co. v. United States (1971), the Supreme Court decided what?
options: The government could not block newspapers from publishing the papers
The papers had to be returned to the Pentagon before publication
The Times was guilty of treason for publishing classified documents
The president could censor newspapers during an undeclared war
questions.explain: The Court held that the government failed to meet its heavy burden for prior restraint, ruling 6 to 3 for the press.

questions.q: What did the Nixon White House do in response to the Pentagon Papers leak?
options: Dissolved the Defense Department's research office
Created a secret "plumbers" unit to stop leaks
Declassified all remaining Vietnam files at once
Opened a congressional inquiry into Pentagon spending
questions.explain: The special unit later broke into the office of Ellsberg's psychiatrist and was connected to the Watergate break-in.

questions.q: The Paris Peace Accords signed in January 1973 provided for what?
options: The permanent division of Vietnam into two separate nations
The unconditional surrender of North Vietnam to the South
Free elections in North Vietnam supervised by the United Nations
A cease-fire and the withdrawal of U.S. forces from Vietnam
questions.explain: The agreement ended direct U.S. combat and returned prisoners of war, but fighting between Vietnamese forces continued.

questions.q: Operation Homecoming, in early 1973, involved what?
options: The return of American prisoners of war from North Vietnam
The evacuation of Americans and allies from Saigon by helicopter
A bombing halt over Hanoi and Haiphong that began peace talks
The release of jailed draft resisters under a general amnesty
questions.explain: Hundreds of American POWs were released after the Paris agreement, many of them airmen who had been held for years.

questions.q: The War Powers Resolution of 1973 required the president to do what?
options: Get a formal declaration of war before sending troops anywhere
Report to the Supreme Court within 48 hours of any deployment
Notify Congress within 48 hours of sending troops into hostilities
End the draft and move to an all-volunteer military force
questions.explain: Congress passed it over Nixon's veto and sought to limit presidents' ability to wage war without legislative approval.

questions.q: The fall of Saigon occurred in what month and year?
options: January 1973
March 1968
August 1964
April 1975
questions.explain: North Vietnamese forces took the capital on April 30, 1975, as the last Americans and many South Vietnamese were evacuated by helicopter.

questions.q: After 1975 many Southeast Asians fled to the United States. What caused their departure?
options: A 1975 change in the quota system favoring Southeast Asians
Communist victories in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia
The Hart-Celler Act of 1965, which opened immigration from Asia
A severe famine across the Philippines and Indonesia
questions.explain: Refugees left by sea and across borders, and Congress passed the Refugee Act of 1980 to create a more regular system of admission.

questions.q: The Vietnam Veterans Memorial was dedicated in what year?
questions.explain: The black granite wall was dedicated in November 1982, after a design competition won by a young architecture student.

questions.q: Whose design won the 1981 national competition for the Vietnam Veterans Memorial?
options: Louis Kahn
I. M. Pei
Maya Lin
Henry Bacon
questions.explain: Lin, then an undergraduate at Yale, won an open competition with a plan for a V-shaped wall of polished black granite.

questions.q: How are the names on the Vietnam Veterans Memorial arranged?
options: By date of casualty
In alphabetical order
By rank and branch
By state of residence
questions.explain: The names begin at the center in 1959, run to the end of the wall, and resume at the start to finish at the center in 1975.

questions.q: Why did Maya Lin's design for the Vietnam Veterans Memorial prove controversial at first?
options: It was built far from the National Mall, away from other memorials
It omitted most names of the war dead, angering families
It was funded entirely by federal money, which angered taxpayers
Some veterans found it too plain and somber, and a statue was added
questions.explain: Critics wanted a more traditional heroic design, and a statue of three servicemen was added nearby in 1984.

questions.q: Visitors to the Vietnam Veterans Memorial often leave items there. What happens to them?
options: They are collected and preserved by the National Park Service
They are removed and thrown away at the end of each day
They are shipped to the Pentagon archives for classified review
They are returned to the senders when addresses can be found
questions.explain: The mementos, from letters to medals, are kept in a collection that helps document how Americans remember the war.

questions.q: About how many names are inscribed on the Vietnam Veterans Memorial?
options: Fewer than 6,000
More than 580,000
More than 58,000
Roughly 128,000
questions.explain: The names of American service members who died or went missing in the war are on the wall, and new names are added when deaths are linked to the war.

questions.q: Who led the effort to build the Vietnam Veterans Memorial and gather funds?
options: Ron Kovic
John Kerry
Colin Powell
Jan Scruggs
questions.explain: Scruggs, a veteran, founded the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund in 1979, and the memorial was paid for by private donations.

questions.q: What motivated the creation of the Vietnam Women's Memorial in 1993?
options: To honor the women, many of them nurses, who served in the war
To honor civilian victims of Agent Orange and napalm in Vietnam
To honor the women who led the antiwar movement at home
To honor the Gold Star mothers of soldiers who died overseas
questions.explain: The sculpture shows three women with a wounded soldier, recognizing contributions that had gone unnoticed.

questions.q: In October 1967, antiwar demonstrators rallied at the Lincoln Memorial and then marched to which building?
options: The White House
The Pentagon
The Capitol
The Treasury
questions.explain: Tens of thousands gathered, and some confronted soldiers guarding the building, an example of the war's growing political divide.

questions.q: In May 1970 President Nixon made an unannounced early-morning visit to which site to talk with antiwar students?
options: Arlington Cemetery
The Washington Monument
The Lincoln Memorial
The Jefferson Memorial
questions.explain: Nixon spoke with students camped in Washington after Kent State and Cambodia, an unusual meeting between a president and protesters.

questions.q: Senator J. William Fulbright's 1966 hearings were important because they did what?
options: Formally declared war against North Vietnam
Authorized another 100,000 troops for deployment
Approved a plan to create the draft lottery
Aired public criticism of the war on television
questions.explain: The Foreign Relations Committee hearings gave a national platform to doubts about Johnson's policy.

questions.q: Robert McNamara served as Secretary of Defense under which two presidents?
options: Eisenhower and Kennedy
Johnson and Nixon
Kennedy and Johnson
Truman and Eisenhower
questions.explain: McNamara oversaw the build-up in Vietnam and later came to doubt the war's course.

questions.q: What does the term "flexible response" describe in Kennedy's defense policy?
options: Avoiding all overseas conflict while keeping troops at home
Preparing for a range of military options, not only nuclear weapons
Relying solely on atomic weapons to deter Soviet attack
Ending NATO commitments in favor of bilateral defense treaties
questions.explain: Kennedy criticized Eisenhower's reliance on nuclear weapons and built up conventional forces and special forces.

questions.q: Eisenhower's strategy of "massive retaliation" meant what?
options: Relying only on conventional forces to deter Soviet attack
Withdrawing American troops from Korea and Western Europe
Disarming unilaterally to encourage Soviet reductions
Threatening an overwhelming nuclear response to aggression
questions.explain: The policy relied on nuclear weapons to deter attack while holding down defense spending.

questions.q: The Cold War idea of "mutually assured destruction" meant that what?
options: Each side could destroy the other, which discouraged nuclear war
The superpowers agreed to share their nuclear weapons with allies
A nuclear war could be won by the side that struck first
All nuclear weapons were banned by treaty in the 1960s
questions.explain: The balance of terror was thought to make a first strike suicidal.

questions.q: Which strategic arms agreement of 1972 limited American and Soviet missile defenses?
options: The START Treaty
The INF Treaty
The SALT II Treaty
The ABM Treaty
questions.explain: SALT I produced the ABM Treaty and an interim limit on offensive missiles, a mark of detente under Nixon and Brezhnev.

questions.q: President Nixon's 1972 trip to China was significant because it did what?
options: Opened the way to relations between Washington and Beijing
