Ended the Vietnam War through a deal with Chinese leaders
Produced a mutual defense treaty with Taiwan's government
Created a formal military alliance against the Soviet Union
questions.explain: It ended more than two decades of American refusal to engage the People's Republic, shifting the balance of the Cold War.

questions.q: Which policy of the 1970s aimed at easing tensions between the superpowers?
options: The policy of rollback
The policy of containment
The policy of detente
The policy of brinkmanship
questions.explain: Nixon and Kissinger pursued arms limits and trade with Moscow even as competition continued.

questions.q: The Helsinki Accords of 1975 included what commitment?
options: The removal of Soviet troops from East Germany
Respect for borders and for human rights
An end to the arms race and a freeze on new missiles
A freeze on new missile deployments in Europe
questions.explain: Thirty-five nations signed; the human rights provisions later gave dissidents in Eastern Europe a basis for criticizing their governments.

questions.q: Why did the United States boycott the 1980 Moscow Olympics?
options: Because of Soviet missile deployments in Cuba
Because of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan
Because of a Soviet nuclear test over the Pacific
Because of the Soviet-backed crackdown in Poland
questions.explain: Jimmy Carter also imposed a grain embargo and asked the Senate to delay action on the SALT II treaty after the Soviets entered Afghanistan.

questions.q: The Iranian hostage crisis began in November 1979 when what happened?
options: Militants seized the U.S. embassy in Tehran
Iran attacked a U.S. Navy ship in the Persian Gulf
Iran cut off oil sales to the United States and Europe
Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz to American ships
questions.explain: Fifty-two Americans were held for 444 days, and the crisis weighed on the Carter presidency.

questions.q: On what date were the American hostages in Iran released?
options: November 4, 1979
April 25, 1980
January 1, 1979
January 20, 1981
questions.explain: They were freed minutes after Ronald Reagan was sworn in, after months of negotiation and a failed rescue attempt.

questions.q: The Camp David Accords of 1978 involved which two leaders?
options: Hafez al-Assad of Syria and Yitzhak Rabin of Israel
King Hussein of Jordan and Golda Meir of Israel
Anwar Sadat of Egypt and Menachem Begin of Israel
Fidel Castro of Cuba and Leonid Brezhnev
questions.explain: Carter brought the leaders together at the presidential retreat and mediated for thirteen days.

questions.q: The Egypt-Israel peace treaty of 1979 was signed where?
options: At Camp David
At the White House
At the United Nations
At the Capitol Rotunda
questions.explain: The treaty came out of the Camp David talks and was signed on the North Lawn, with Carter, Sadat, and Begin.

questions.q: What was the effect of the 1977 Panama Canal treaties?
options: They provided for Panama to take control of the canal by 1999
They returned the canal to Colombia, which had once owned it
They permanently closed the canal to American warships
They set up a joint free-trade zone along the canal route
questions.explain: The Senate ratified them narrowly in 1978 after heated debate.

questions.q: Carter's foreign policy was known for emphasizing what?
options: Rolling back communism
Nuclear brinkmanship
Strict isolationism
Promoting human rights
questions.explain: Carter linked aid and diplomacy to the treatment of citizens abroad, though critics said it was applied unevenly.

questions.q: The Carter Doctrine of 1980 declared what?
options: The U.S. would withdraw its forces from Asia and the Middle East
Congress would take over control of all arms sales abroad
The U.S. would use force to defend its interests in the Persian Gulf
The Soviet Union would be a partner in securing Gulf oil
questions.explain: It was a response to the Soviet move into Afghanistan and the importance of Gulf oil.

questions.q: Which president was buried at Arlington National Cemetery in November 1963, under an eternal flame?
options: Franklin Roosevelt
John F. Kennedy
Herbert Hoover
Dwight Eisenhower
questions.explain: Kennedy was killed in Dallas on November 22, and his grave site includes the flame lit by his widow.

questions.q: Where did John F. Kennedy's body lie in state in 1963?
options: The Capitol Rotunda
The Lincoln Memorial
The Supreme Court
The National Cathedral
questions.explain: Hundreds of thousands filed past the flag-draped coffin, before the funeral at St. Matthew's Cathedral and burial at Arlington.

questions.q: Which commission investigated the assassination of President Kennedy?
options: The Kerner Commission
The Church Committee
The Warren Commission
The Tower Commission
questions.explain: Chief Justice Earl Warren led it, and it concluded in 1964 that Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone.

questions.q: Where did Lyndon Johnson take the oath of office after Kennedy's death?
options: In the Capitol Rotunda
On the White House lawn
At Parkland Memorial Hospital
Aboard Air Force One at Dallas
questions.explain: Judge Sarah Hughes administered the oath on the plane, with Jacqueline Kennedy standing beside him.

questions.q: Who is honored at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery?
options: Unidentified American service members from wars
Presidents who also served as military officers
Only soldiers killed in World War I battles
Allied soldiers killed fighting alongside Americans
questions.explain: Unknowns from World War I, World War II, and Korea were interred there, and a Vietnam Unknown was interred in 1984.

questions.q: What happened to the Vietnam War Unknown interred at Arlington in 1984?
options: His remains were moved to the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in 1990
He remained unidentified and the crypt is still occupied
His remains were relocated to Punchbowl cemetery in Hawaii in 1995
His remains were identified in 1998 and returned to his family
questions.explain: DNA testing identified Air Force Lt. Michael Blassie, and the crypt for the Vietnam Unknown was left empty.

questions.q: Civil rights leader Medgar Evers, killed in 1963, was buried where?
options: Tuskegee National Cemetery
Arlington National Cemetery
Atlanta's Westview Cemetery
Jackson's Greenwood Cemetery
questions.explain: As a veteran of World War II, he was entitled to burial at Arlington, where his grave draws visitors.

questions.q: Robert F. Kennedy, assassinated in 1968, is buried where?
options: Holyhood Cemetery in Brookline
Hollywood Forever Cemetery
Arlington National Cemetery
St. Patrick's Cathedral, New York
questions.explain: He was buried near his brother, John, on the cemetery's hillside.

questions.q: Which Apollo 1 astronauts are buried at Arlington National Cemetery?
options: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin
Deke Slayton and Scott Carpenter
Gus Grissom and Roger Chaffee
Jim Lovell and Jack Swigert
questions.explain: The two were killed in the 1967 launch pad fire; the third crew member, Ed White, is buried at West Point.

questions.q: Arlington National Cemetery sits on land that was once owned by which Confederate general's family?
options: Stonewall Jackson
James Longstreet
Jubal Early
Robert E. Lee
questions.explain: The Union seized the Arlington estate during the Civil War, and the grounds became a military cemetery.

questions.q: Which law of 1964, passed as part of the War on Poverty, created the Office of Economic Opportunity?
options: The Economic Opportunity Act
The Higher Education Act
The Social Security Amendments
The Appalachian Regional Act
questions.explain: Johnson announced the War on Poverty in 1964, and the act funded programs such as Job Corps and Head Start.

questions.q: Which two health programs created in 1965 cover older adults and low-income people?
options: Social Security and SSI
Medicare and Medicaid
Head Start and Job Corps
WIC and school lunches
questions.explain: Medicare covers people 65 and older, and Medicaid is a joint federal-state program for people with low incomes.

questions.q: Which Great Society law of 1965 increased federal aid to public schools, mostly for poor districts?
options: The Elementary and Secondary Education Act
The National Defense Education Act
The Higher Education Facilities Act
The Education for All Handicapped Children Act
questions.explain: The law funded textbooks and programs aimed at disadvantaged children.

questions.q: What was Head Start?
options: A job training program for unemployed urban young adults
A preschool program for children from low-income families
A program granting draft deferments to college freshmen
A federal highway plan linking rural towns to cities
questions.explain: Head Start, launched in 1965 as part of Lyndon Johnson's War on Poverty, offers preschool, meals and health services to children from low-income families.

questions.q: Lyndon Johnson's domestic agenda of the mid-1960s was known by what name?
options: The New Frontier
The Square Deal
The Great Society
The New Federalism
questions.explain: Johnson aimed to end poverty and racial injustice, and Congress passed many laws after his landslide win in 1964.

questions.q: Which book by Michael Harrington helped draw attention to poverty in the early 1960s?
options: The Affluent Society
The Feminine Mystique
The Lonely Crowd
The Other America
questions.explain: Harrington's 1962 study argued that tens of millions of Americans lived in poverty even in a prosperous nation.

questions.q: The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 changed American immigration policy by doing what?
options: Banning most immigration from Asia and Africa
Ending the national-origins quota system
Creating a new guest-worker program for farm laborers
Eliminating family ties as a basis for admission
questions.explain: The law favored family ties and skills and, over time, brought many more immigrants from Asia and Latin America.

questions.q: What was the 1964 Wilderness Act intended to do?
options: Protect designated federal lands from development
Open public wilderness areas to commercial mining
Create the National Park Service and its first parks
Tax lumber companies on timber cut from federal lands
questions.explain: The law set aside millions of acres where nature was to remain largely untouched.

questions.q: The National Foundation on the Arts and the Humanities, created in 1965, did what?
options: Created the Library of Congress as a national archive
Banned the sale of works judged obscene by local boards
Required stations to carry public broadcasting programs
Provided federal funding for the arts and humanities
questions.explain: The act set up the National Endowments for the Arts and the Humanities.

questions.q: In Gideon v. Wainwright (1963), the Supreme Court ruled that what?
options: Police must read suspects their rights before questioning them
Evidence from illegal searches could not be used in state courts
States must provide lawyers to felony defendants who cannot afford one
Juries in state felony trials must reach unanimous verdicts
questions.explain: The Court said the Sixth Amendment right to counsel applies to states under the 14th Amendment.

questions.q: Miranda v. Arizona (1966) required police to do what?
options: Provide a lawyer to every suspect at the moment of arrest
Inform suspects of their rights before questioning in custody
Obtain a judge's warrant before making any arrest in public
Record every interrogation of suspects on audio or video
questions.explain: The warnings include the right to remain silent and the right to an attorney.

questions.q: Mapp v. Ohio (1961) extended which rule to the states?
options: The right to a trial by jury in all criminal cases
The right to keep and bear arms at home
The exclusionary rule barring illegally obtained evidence
Freedom of the press from prior restraint by state officials
questions.explain: Evidence seized in violation of the Fourth Amendment could not be used in state courts.

questions.q: Engel v. Vitale (1962) ruled what about public schools?
options: Officially sponsored prayer violates the Establishment Clause
Daily Bible reading is required in every public school
Schools may teach religion as part of the regular curriculum
Prayer is allowed if it is voluntary and nondenominational
questions.explain: The Court held that a state-written prayer in public schools was unconstitutional, even though students could opt out.

questions.q: The "one person, one vote" principle came from which Supreme Court cases of the 1960s?
options: Brown v. Board and Cooper v. Aaron
Mapp v. Ohio and Gideon v. Wainwright
Roe v. Wade and Doe v. Bolton
Baker v. Carr and Reynolds v. Sims
questions.explain: The Court held that legislative districts must be roughly equal in population, which increased urban and suburban representation.

questions.q: Griswold v. Connecticut (1965) is best known for what ruling?
options: A right of privacy protects married couples' use of contraception
A right of privacy made abortion legal in the first trimester
Women had a constitutional right to equal pay for equal work
Teachers could not lead organized prayer in public schools
questions.explain: The justices found a right to privacy implied by several amendments, and it later underlay other decisions.

questions.q: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), the Supreme Court ruled that students had what right?
options: To be exempt from the draft while enrolled in high school
To wear black armbands in school as symbolic protest
To ignore any school dress code limiting self-expression
To publish any article in the school paper without review
questions.explain: Students do not shed their free speech rights at the schoolhouse gate, unless the speech substantially disrupts school.

questions.q: New York Times v. Sullivan (1964) made it harder for public officials to win libel suits by requiring what?
options: A written retraction
A federal indictment
Proof of actual malice
Proof of financial loss
questions.explain: The Court said criticism of officials is protected unless the statement was knowingly false or made with reckless disregard for the truth.

questions.q: Which chief justice presided over the Supreme Court from 1953 to 1969, a period of expanded rights?
options: Warren Burger
Fred Vinson
Harlan F. Stone
Earl Warren
questions.explain: His Court decided Brown, Gideon, and Miranda, and critics sometimes called for his impeachment.

questions.q: Which president appointed Warren Burger as Chief Justice in 1969?
options: Lyndon Johnson
Richard Nixon
John F. Kennedy
Gerald Ford
questions.explain: Nixon, who had campaigned on appointing justices who would interpret the Constitution strictly, named four justices in his first term.

questions.q: The Watergate scandal began with what event in June 1972?
options: The leak of the Pentagon Papers to The New York Times
A bombing of a federal office building in Washington
A break-in at the Democratic National Committee headquarters
An FBI raid on the Republican National Committee offices
questions.explain: Five men tied to President Nixon's reelection committee were arrested at the Watergate office complex in Washington.

questions.q: Which two Washington Post reporters investigated the Watergate scandal?
options: Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein
Walter Cronkite and Dan Rather
Neil Sheehan and Hedrick Smith
Edward R. Murrow and Eric Sevareid
questions.explain: Their reporting, aided by an anonymous source, linked the break-in to the White House and the campaign.

questions.q: Which Senate committee, led by Sam Ervin, held televised hearings on Watergate in 1973?
options: The Senate Judiciary Committee on Federal Election Practices
The Armed Services Committee on Executive Intelligence
The Foreign Relations Committee on White House Conduct
The Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities
questions.explain: The hearings drew a large television audience and exposed White House efforts to cover up the break-in.

questions.q: What did White House aide Alexander Butterfield reveal to the Senate Watergate committee in July 1973?
options: That Nixon had personally ordered the Watergate break-in
That the reelection campaign had taken illegal foreign funds
That the FBI had secretly wiretapped several news reporters
That Nixon had a secret taping system in the White House
questions.explain: His disclosure led to a fight over access to the tapes that ended in the Supreme Court.

questions.q: What was the "Saturday Night Massacre" of October 1973?
options: Nixon's firing of the special prosecutor and the resignations of top Justice Department officials
Nixon's dismissal of the FBI director and the resignation of the White House counsel and chief of staff
The firing of the Senate committee's chief counsel and the resignation of several Republican members
The removal of the Watergate judge and the resignations of two Supreme Court justices
questions.explain: After Nixon ordered Archibald Cox fired, Attorney General Elliot Richardson and his deputy left, and the public reaction to the dismissals was strong.

questions.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in United States v. Nixon (1974)?
options: The president held absolute executive privilege over all White House tapes
The president had to turn over the tapes to the special prosecutor
The tapes were Nixon's private property and could be kept from Congress
The Court lacked power to hear a dispute inside the executive branch
questions.explain: The unanimous ruling said executive privilege exists but is not absolute against a criminal subpoena.

questions.q: Which committee of the House voted in July 1974 to recommend articles of impeachment against Nixon?
options: The Ways and Means Committee
The Rules Committee
The Judiciary Committee
The Foreign Affairs Committee
questions.explain: It approved articles charging obstruction of justice, abuse of power, and contempt of Congress, though the full House never voted.

questions.q: When did Richard Nixon resign the presidency?
options: January 1973
November 1972
August 1974
April 1975
questions.explain: Facing near-certain impeachment after the release of a tape linking him to the cover-up, Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974.

questions.q: Which president took office when Richard Nixon resigned?
options: Nelson Rockefeller
Gerald Ford
Spiro Agnew
Hubert Humphrey
questions.explain: Ford was the first person to become president without winning a national election for either president or vice president.

questions.q: How did Gerald Ford become the first vice president chosen under the 25th Amendment?
options: Nixon resigned in 1974 and Ford was elected in a special vote by the Electoral College
Hubert Humphrey died in 1973 and Ford was named by the Senate alone
Agnew was impeached in 1973 and Ford won a special nationwide election
Spiro Agnew resigned in 1973 and Ford was appointed with Congress's approval
questions.explain: The amendment, ratified in 1967, lets presidents fill a vice presidency with the consent of both houses.

questions.q: What controversial action did Gerald Ford take in September 1974?
options: He pardoned Richard Nixon
He ended the military draft
He fired his entire cabinet
He called a snap election
questions.explain: Ford said the pardon would help the nation move on; critics questioned it, and his approval rating dropped sharply.

questions.q: The Nixon tapes are important to historians because they do what?
options: Record every diplomatic meeting from Nixon's trip to China
Reveal the secret vote counts in the 1972 election
Provide direct evidence of conversations in the Oval Office
Document the planning of the Apollo moon program
questions.explain: The tapes, held by the National Archives, captured discussions of the cover-up, including the "smoking gun" conversation of June 1972.

questions.q: Congress passed the Presidential Records Act in 1978 to do what?
options: Make presidential papers public property after a president leaves office
Allow presidents to keep or destroy their papers after leaving office
Give outgoing presidents full control of their private records and tapes
Require each president to tape-record all Oval Office meetings for archives
questions.explain: It followed the dispute over Nixon's tapes and put presidential records under the control of the National Archives.

questions.q: The Church Committee of 1975 investigated what?
options: The Watergate break-in and cover-up
Waste in the Vietnam War budget
Bribery in the Teapot Dome scandal
Abuses by U.S. intelligence agencies
questions.explain: The Senate committee found that the CIA and FBI had spied on Americans and plotted against foreign leaders, and it led to new oversight.

questions.q: The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 set up what?
options: A ban on all wiretaps of suspected foreign agents on U.S. soil
A court to approve some surveillance of suspected foreign agents
A national identification system for tracking visitors from abroad
A new Pentagon bureau that directed overseas spying operations
questions.explain: The law answered abuses revealed in the 1970s by requiring judicial approval of certain surveillance.

questions.q: In Buckley v. Valeo (1976), the Supreme Court held what about campaign finance?
options: All limits on contributions and spending were unconstitutional
All limits on contributions and spending were constitutional
Only political parties could donate to federal candidates
Limits on contributions were allowed but limits on spending were not
questions.explain: The Court treated spending money on political speech as protected, but accepted limits on contributions to prevent corruption.

questions.q: Which law of 1974 created contribution limits and the Federal Election Commission in response to Watergate?
options: The Federal Election Campaign Act amendments
The Hatch Act amendments, which barred federal employees from campaigning
The McCain-Feingold Act, which banned soft money in federal campaigns
The Pendleton Act, which created a merit-based federal civil service
questions.explain: Lawmakers sought to limit big donations after revelations about the 1972 campaign.

questions.q: The 1973 oil embargo by Arab members of OPEC was a response to what?
options: The Iranian revolution and the fall of the Shah that same year
The Apollo moon landing program's heavy use of petroleum fuels
U.S. support for Israel in the Yom Kippur War
The Vietnam peace talks and the withdrawal of American troops
questions.explain: Oil prices soared and Americans waited in long lines at gas stations.

questions.q: Which measure did Congress approve in 1974 in response to the energy crisis?
options: A national ban on all imports of oil from Arab countries
A national speed limit of 55 miles per hour
A federal gasoline tax of one dollar per gallon on motorists
A nationwide halt to commercial air travel on weekends
questions.explain: The limit was meant to save fuel and remained in place until the 1990s.

questions.q: What does the term "stagflation" describe?
options: Falling prices combined with rapid economic growth and low unemployment
High inflation combined with slow growth and high unemployment
Rising stock prices combined with steady wages and low inflation
A federal budget surplus combined with falling interest rates
questions.explain: The 1970s combination puzzled economists, who had thought inflation and unemployment moved in opposite directions.

questions.q: In August 1971, President Nixon announced which policy that effectively ended the Bretton Woods system?
options: Raising the official price of gold to $70 an ounce
Creating a new international currency backed by silver
Banning foreign investment in American companies
Suspending the dollar's convertibility into gold
questions.explain: Nixon also ordered a wage and price freeze and a surcharge on imports.

questions.q: Under the Bretton Woods system, what was the value of the dollar tied to?
options: Gold, with other currencies tied to the dollar
Silver, with other currencies tied to the pound
The British pound, with the dollar tied to sterling
Oil, with other currencies tied to Saudi production
questions.explain: The dollar was convertible at $35 an ounce, and the arrangement lasted until the early 1970s.

questions.q: President Ford's "WIN" campaign of 1974 urged Americans to do what?
options: Win the space race through science education
Win elections by volunteering for candidates
Whip inflation now through voluntary measures
Weigh imports now through voluntary quotas
questions.explain: The campaign relied on buttons and pledges, but it had little effect on prices.

questions.q: Which industry did the Carter administration and Congress deregulate in 1978?
options: Banking
Railroads
Airlines
Utilities
questions.explain: The Airline Deregulation Act ended federal control of fares and routes, and prices fell for many travelers.

questions.q: Which Federal Reserve chairman raised interest rates sharply from 1979 to curb inflation?
options: Alan Greenspan
Paul Volcker
Ben Bernanke
Arthur Burns
questions.explain: The policy brought a deep recession in the early 1980s, but inflation fell sharply.

questions.q: California's Proposition 13 in 1978 is often cited as a sign of what trend?
options: A new environmental movement
A school desegregation drive
A welfare expansion
A growing tax revolt
questions.explain: The measure capped property taxes and encouraged similar moves in other states.

questions.q: The Department of Energy, created in 1977, was established under which president?
options: Jimmy Carter
Richard Nixon
Gerald Ford
Lyndon Johnson
questions.explain: Carter made energy policy a priority and called the energy crisis the "moral equivalent of war."

questions.q: Which incident in March 1979 raised public fear about nuclear power?
options: The fire at the Chernobyl reactor in the Soviet Union
The accident at Three Mile Island
The Santa Barbara oil spill off the California coast
The Cuyahoga River fire in Ohio
questions.explain: A partial meltdown in Pennsylvania caused no known deaths but slowed the building of new reactors.

questions.q: Which 1963 book by Betty Friedan questioned the idea that women found fulfillment only as housewives?
options: Silent Spring, by Rachel Carson
The Other America, by Michael Harrington
Unsafe at Any Speed, by Ralph Nader
The Feminine Mystique
questions.explain: Friedan described the "problem that has no name" and helped launch the modern women's movement.

questions.q: What was the National Organization for Women (NOW), founded in 1966?
options: A group seeking full equality for women in work and law
A temperance league urging women to oppose alcohol
A labor union representing hospital nurses nationwide
A new political party running women for Congress
questions.explain: Friedan and others founded NOW to act as a civil rights group for women, pressing for enforcement of the new law against job discrimination.

questions.q: The Equal Pay Act of 1963 required what?
options: A higher minimum wage for women in industrial jobs
Paid maternity leave for women in federal employment
Equal pay for men and women doing the same work
Equal hiring quotas for men and women in large firms
questions.explain: The act did not end the wage gap, but it made unequal pay for equal work illegal.

questions.q: Which 1972 law banned sex discrimination in federally funded education programs, including athletics?
options: Title VII
The Equal Rights Amendment
Title IX
The Civil Rights Act of 1968
questions.explain: Title IX of the Education Amendments led to a large increase in women's sports participation.

questions.q: What was the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA), which Congress sent to the states in 1972?
options: A proposed constitutional amendment banning sex discrimination
A federal law requiring equal pay for equal work by employers
A plan for publicly funded child care for working mothers
A proposed amendment protecting a woman's right to an abortion
questions.explain: It said that equality of rights could not be denied on account of sex, and it needed approval of three-fourths of the states.

questions.q: What happened to the Equal Rights Amendment by the deadline set by Congress?
options: It was ratified by all fifty states
It fell short of the 38 states needed
It was rejected by a vote in the Senate
It was declared void by the Supreme Court
questions.explain: Thirty-five states ratified it by the extended 1982 deadline, and some states later voted to rescind their approval.

questions.q: Who led the STOP ERA campaign that opposed the amendment in the 1970s?
options: Gloria Steinem, of Ms.
Betty Friedan, of NOW
Bella Abzug, of New York
Phyllis Schlafly
questions.explain: Schlafly argued that the amendment would remove protections for women and mobilized conservative activists.

questions.q: Roe v. Wade (1973) was a Supreme Court decision about what?
options: Whether public schools could sponsor organized prayer in classrooms
Whether states could use literacy tests to restrict voting rights
Whether federal courts could order busing to achieve school integration
Whether the Constitution protected a woman's right to choose an abortion
questions.explain: The Court held in 1973 that a right to privacy covered the decision, subject to state interests that grew as pregnancy advanced.

questions.q: By what vote did the Supreme Court decide Roe v. Wade in 1973?
options: 5 to 4
7 to 2
9 to 0
6 to 3
questions.explain: Justice Harry Blackmun wrote the majority opinion, and Justices White and Rehnquist dissented.

questions.q: Roe v. Wade was decided in what year?
questions.explain: The decision came just after Congress sent the Equal Rights Amendment to the states, in a period of intense debate about women's roles.

questions.q: Which 1960 development gave women greater control over family planning?
options: A federal child-care law for working mothers
Passage of the Equal Pay Act
FDA approval of the birth control pill
Congressional approval of the ERA
questions.explain: The pill became available in the early 1960s, and its use spread quickly after Griswold removed legal barriers for married couples.

questions.q: The 1978 Pregnancy Discrimination Act did what?
options: Guaranteed twelve weeks of paid family leave
Made contraception free under federal insurance
Created a national system of child care centers
Banned job discrimination based on pregnancy
questions.explain: It amended Title VII to treat pregnancy-related conditions as covered by the ban on sex discrimination.

questions.q: Which event of June 1969 in New York City is widely seen as a turning point for the gay rights movement?
options: The Stonewall uprising
The Selma march
The Haymarket riot
The Woodstock festival
questions.explain: Patrons and neighbors resisted a police raid at a Greenwich Village bar, and annual marches began the next year.

questions.q: Which two organizers built the United Farm Workers union in the 1960s?
options: Eugene Debs and Mother Jones
Asa Philip Randolph and Walter Reuther
Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta
John L. Lewis and Samuel Gompers
questions.explain: Chavez and Huerta built the United Farm Workers, using strikes and boycotts to win contracts for farm workers.

questions.q: The farm workers' boycott of California grapes was designed to do what?
options: Raise grape prices by cutting the national supply
Pressure growers to sign union contracts by reducing sales
Support imported Chilean grapes over California crops
Force a ban on pesticides through a state referendum
questions.explain: Supporters across the nation refused to buy grapes, and in 1970 major growers signed contracts.

questions.q: What were the 1968 "walkouts" or "blowouts" in East Los Angeles?
options: Strikes by farm workers against California grape growers
Student protests against unequal schools for Mexican Americans
Riots that followed a police shooting in East Los Angeles
A boycott of the city's public bus system by Latino riders
questions.explain: Thousands of students demanded better education and bilingual teaching, part of the broader Chicano movement.

questions.q: The American Indian Movement (AIM), founded in 1968, sought to do what?
options: End all federal aid to tribes and close reservations
Relocate tribes to cities under federal programs
Merge with the Black Panthers as a single party
Defend Native rights and sovereignty and protest abuses
questions.explain: AIM began in Minneapolis, in part to oppose police harassment of Native people in cities, and it took up treaty rights.

questions.q: What was the 1969-1971 occupation of Alcatraz Island?
options: A prison escape that led to a long standoff with the Coast Guard
A sit-in by Bay Area college students against the Vietnam War
A protest by Native Americans who claimed the island under a treaty
A military drill by National Guard units on the former prison island
questions.explain: Activists called Indians of All Tribes held the island for 19 months, drawing public attention to Native issues.

questions.q: In November 1972, the "Trail of Broken Treaties" caravan took which action in Washington?
options: Occupying the Bureau of Indian Affairs headquarters
Marching in a large rally at the Lincoln Memorial
Holding a negotiating meeting with the president at Camp David
Entering the Senate chamber to present a petition
questions.explain: Native activists traveled to the capital with a list of demands and occupied the building for several days.

questions.q: Where did members of AIM and Oglala Lakota take over a town in 1973 in a 71-day standoff?
options: Alcatraz Island, California
Selma, Alabama, on Highway 80
Little Rock, Arkansas, in 1957
Wounded Knee, South Dakota
questions.explain: The standoff took place at the site of the 1890 massacre, and it drew federal marshals and the FBI.

questions.q: Why was Wounded Knee a symbolic site for the 1973 protest?
options: It was the location of an 1890 massacre of Lakota people
It was the site of a famous 1836 siege in Texas
It held the main Bureau of Indian Affairs office
It was where the Lakota treaties were signed in 1868
questions.explain: The protesters called attention to treaties and tribal governance on the Pine Ridge Reservation, where the 1890 killings took place.

questions.q: The federal "termination" policy of the 1950s sought to do what?
options: Give tribes more land and wider powers of self-government
Create new reservations for tribes in the Western states
End the federal government's recognition of some tribes
Convert tribal lands into new territories seeking statehood
questions.explain: Congress ended federal relations with more than a hundred tribes, and many lost land and services.

questions.q: Which 1975 law allowed tribes to manage federal programs for themselves?
options: The Dawes General Allotment Act, which divided tribal lands
The Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act
The Indian Reorganization Act, which ended allotment in 1934
The Indian Removal Act, which sent tribes west of the Mississippi
questions.explain: The act marked a shift away from termination and toward tribal control of programs for health and schooling.

questions.q: Which 1968 law extended parts of the Bill of Rights to tribal governments' dealings with individuals?
options: The Indian Citizenship Act, which granted citizenship in 1924
The Indian Civil Rights Act
The Dawes Act, which divided reservation land into allotments
The Wheeler-Howard Act, which set up tribal constitutions
questions.explain: The act applied many rights to people under tribal authority, though it limited some tribal powers.

questions.q: The National Museum of the American Indian opened on the National Mall in what year?
questions.explain: It was created by Congress in 1989 and tells the history and cultures of Native peoples of the Western Hemisphere.

questions.q: Rachel Carson's 1962 book Silent Spring warned of the dangers of what?
options: Nuclear fallout from weapons tests
Air pollution from automobiles
Offshore oil drilling
Pesticides such as DDT
questions.explain: Carson argued that chemicals were harming birds and other wildlife, and the book spurred a national debate.

questions.q: The Environmental Protection Agency was created in 1970 during the administration of which president?
options: Lyndon Johnson
Jimmy Carter
Richard Nixon
Dwight Eisenhower
questions.explain: Nixon proposed the agency to combine federal pollution programs, and it began work in December 1970.

questions.q: The first Earth Day, held in April 1970, was notable because it did what?
options: Created the Environmental Protection Agency by presidential decree
Drew millions of Americans to events on the environment
Banned the use of the pesticide DDT across the United States
Led Congress to pass the Clean Air Act within the same week
questions.explain: Organizers estimated about twenty million people took part, which helped build support for new laws.

questions.q: The National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 required what?
options: Automakers to install catalytic converters on all new cars by 1972
A nationwide ban on the use of the pesticide DDT on farms
Federal agencies to prepare environmental impact statements
The creation of dozens of new national parks and wilderness areas
questions.explain: The law required review of the environmental effects of major federal actions.

questions.q: The Clean Water Act of 1972 aimed to do what?
options: Fund new hydroelectric dams along the nation's major rivers
End commercial fishing along the Atlantic and Pacific coasts
Ban the sale of bottled water and fund public fountains
Limit pollution discharged into the nation's waters
questions.explain: It set standards for discharges from factories and sewage plants, and required permits.

questions.q: The Endangered Species Act of 1973 did what?
options: Protected species threatened with extinction and their habitats
Banned zoos and private owners from keeping wild animals in captivity
Ended all hunting on federal lands and in national forests
Created a federal tax on products made from wildlife
questions.explain: The law allowed species to be listed and protected from harm by federal law.

questions.q: Which 1969 events helped build support for environmental laws?
options: The Dust Bowl dust storms and the Johnstown Flood of 1889
Three Mile Island and the Chernobyl reactor accident
The Exxon Valdez oil spill and Hurricane Katrina
The Santa Barbara oil spill and a fire on the Cuyahoga River
questions.explain: Images of oil-soaked beaches and a burning river showed the cost of pollution to the public.

questions.q: Which 1980 law, known as Superfund, was created to clean up hazardous waste sites?
options: The Clean Air Act
The Wilderness Act
CERCLA
The Endangered Species Act
questions.explain: It followed the discovery of toxic waste at Love Canal in New York, and it let the government seek payment from polluters.

questions.q: What was the Alaska pipeline, authorized by Congress in 1973?
options: A line carrying oil from the North Slope to the southern coast
A natural gas line running from the North Slope into Canada
A water supply line serving the city of Anchorage and its suburbs
A railway carrying coal from interior Alaska to Pacific ports
questions.explain: The oil crisis helped win approval, and the pipeline began operating in 1977.

questions.q: The Students for a Democratic Society issued which 1962 statement of New Left ideals?
options: The Sharon Statement
The Port Huron Statement
The Seneca Falls Declaration
The Mayflower Compact
questions.explain: It called for participatory democracy and criticized racism, poverty, and the Cold War arms race.

questions.q: The Free Speech Movement of 1964 began at which university?
options: Columbia University in New York City
Harvard University in Massachusetts
University of California, Berkeley
Kent State University in Ohio
questions.explain: Students protested restrictions on political activity on campus, and the movement inspired other student protests.

questions.q: Which 1969 music festival in New York drew roughly 400,000 people and became a symbol of the counterculture?
options: Monterey Pop
Altamont
Newport Folk
Woodstock
questions.explain: Billed as three days of peace and music in mid-August, the festival on a dairy farm in Bethel, upstate New York, ran into a fourth morning and featured rock and folk performers.

questions.q: What is a feature of the 1960s counterculture?
options: Rejection of mainstream values in favor of communal living and experimentation
Strong support for the Vietnam War and for voluntary military service
Loyalty to traditional institutions and established churches and schools
A mass return to farm life by most young Americans in the cities
questions.explain: Participants often called hippies challenged conformity, and the movement affected music, dress, and attitudes.

questions.q: What event in February 1964 helped launch the British Invasion in American popular music?
options: The release of Elvis Presley's first album on RCA Victor
The Beatles' appearance on The Ed Sullivan Show
The Newport Folk Festival in Rhode Island
The Woodstock concert in upstate New York
questions.explain: About 73 million viewers watched the band on television, and British groups became popular in the United States.

questions.q: Rock and roll in the 1950s was significant because it did what?
options: Replaced television as the main form of family entertainment across the South
Won the approval of most parents and church leaders across the country
Appealed mainly to older listeners in rural areas of the South and Midwest
Blended Black rhythm and blues with white country styles and appealed to teenagers
questions.explain: Artists such as Chuck Berry and Elvis Presley helped create a youth culture and crossed racial lines in audience if not in society.

questions.q: What was Motown, founded in Detroit in 1959?
options: A car company that built small economy cars in Michigan
A record label that brought Black artists to a wide audience
A civil rights group that organized boycotts in Detroit
A radio network that served Midwestern cities and towns
questions.explain: Berry Gordy's label produced hit records for acts such as the Supremes and the Temptations.

questions.q: Beat writers of the 1950s, such as Allen Ginsberg and Jack Kerouac, are known for what?
options: Celebrating suburban life and corporate success in postwar America
Writing patriotic works in support of the early Cold War
Criticizing conformity and materialism in postwar society
Promoting science education in the nation's public schools
questions.explain: Works such as Howl and On the Road helped inspire the counterculture of the next decade.

questions.q: How did the growth of television change politics by the 1960s?
options: It brought events like Birmingham and Vietnam into homes and shaped opinion
It reduced public interest in presidential elections after the 1950s
It replaced newspapers as the only trusted source of campaign news
It was banned from covering the national party conventions in 1960
questions.explain: Images of the civil rights struggle and war footage reached millions, which moved opinion and put pressure on officials.

questions.q: Which program, aired in 1977, drew a huge audience and sparked national interest in African American family history?
options: The Cosby Show
Sesame Street
Roots
I Love Lucy
questions.explain: The miniseries, based on a novel by Alex Haley, was watched by an estimated majority of television households.

questions.q: Which National Museum of American History collection reflects 1970s television culture?
options: The chairs of Archie Bunker from All in the Family
The Wright Flyer of 1903, flown at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina
Thomas Edison's early tinfoil phonograph from the 1870s
Abraham Lincoln's top hat from Ford's Theatre in 1865
questions.explain: The chairs from the popular series, which dealt with issues of class and race, are preserved as cultural objects.

questions.q: What object from a famous American kitchen is displayed at the National Museum of American History?
options: The kitchen of Thomas Jefferson
The kitchen of Julia Child
The kitchen of Betsy Ross
The kitchen of Mamie Eisenhower
questions.explain: Child's television cooking show helped change American eating habits, and her Cambridge kitchen was moved to the museum.

questions.q: The development of the transistor at Bell Labs in 1947 was important because it did what?
options: Created the first commercial television broadcasts to homes
Powered the first mass-produced electric cars in America
Replaced telephone lines with long-distance radio links
Led to smaller, cheaper electronics and eventually computers
questions.explain: The device replaced bulky vacuum tubes and made possible the miniaturization of electronic devices.

questions.q: What was ENIAC, unveiled in 1946?
options: A long-range military aircraft built for the Navy after the war
A radio telescope built to track Soviet signals in orbit
One of the first general-purpose electronic digital computers
The first weather satellite launched into orbit by the United States
questions.explain: It filled a large room and was built at the University of Pennsylvania, at first to calculate artillery firing tables.

questions.q: What was ARPANET, which began operating in 1969?
options: A computer network funded by the Defense Department that linked research sites
A satellite system funded by NASA to relay telephone calls across oceans
A cable television service financed by private investors in New York
A telephone network created after the breakup of AT&T
questions.explain: It used packet switching and became a forerunner of the internet.

questions.q: What was the Intel 4004, introduced in 1971?
options: The first transistor
The first commercial microprocessor, a computer processor on a single chip
The first communications satellite
The first electronic digital computer
questions.explain: Intel's 4004 put a computer's central processing unit on one chip, a step that later made small, affordable computers possible.

questions.q: Which company began selling a personal computer designed by Steve Wozniak in 1977?
options: IBM, the maker of mainframe computers
Intel, the maker of microprocessors
Atari, the maker of video games
Apple Computer
questions.explain: The Apple II was one of the first successful mass-produced personal computers; Wozniak designed it and co-founded the company with Steve Jobs.

questions.q: Why did the "Sunbelt" grow rapidly in the postwar decades?
options: Federal limits on migration drew many residents to the Northeast and Midwest
Air conditioning, defense jobs, and warm weather drew people to the South and West
New farmland openings drew large numbers of families to the Great Plains
Free irrigation water drew many settlers to the desert Southwest
questions.explain: Federal defense spending and new industries, along with a growing retiree population, helped the states of the Sunbelt grow.

questions.q: What development of the 1950s made it easier for people to buy goods on credit?
options: A return to the gold standard
A series of national bank holidays
The first widely used credit cards
New federal price controls
questions.explain: The Diners Club card began in 1950, and consumer borrowing grew along with spending.

questions.q: Which businessman expanded McDonald's into a national franchise chain beginning in 1955?
options: Walt Disney
Sam Walton
Henry Ford
Ray Kroc
questions.explain: Kroc's franchise system, with standardized food and service, became a symbol of postwar consumer culture.

questions.q: Which vaccine, announced as safe and effective in 1955, helped end polio epidemics?
options: Jonas Salk's
Albert Sabin's
Louis Pasteur's
Edward Jenner's
questions.explain: Millions of children were vaccinated, and cases of the disease fell sharply.

questions.q: What did the term "military-industrial complex" refer to?
options: A new network of military bases built across the Sunbelt
A weapons treaty between the United States and the Soviet Union
The Pentagon's expanded office space in Arlington, Virginia
The close connection between the armed forces and defense contractors
questions.explain: Eisenhower used it in 1961 to describe how permanent arms production had changed the economy and politics.

questions.q: Which 1970 law created Amtrak?
options: The Interstate Highway Act of 1956
The Rail Passenger Service Act
The Clean Air Act of 1970
The Airline Deregulation Act of 1978
questions.explain: Congress created a national rail passenger corporation to take over failing private railroads, and service began in 1971.

questions.q: Which core idea of supply-side economics guided Ronald Reagan's tax policy in the early 1980s?
options: Raising corporate taxes would curb inflation and stabilize prices
Increased government spending alone could end recessions without tax changes
Cutting tax rates would encourage investment and growth
Tariff revenue would pay down the national debt within a decade
questions.explain: Supporters argued that lower rates would spur work and investment, and critics warned the cuts would enlarge the deficit.

questions.q: The Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 did what?
options: Cut individual income tax rates across the board
Raised the corporate tax rate to fund defense spending
Created the first permanent federal income tax
Eliminated the Social Security payroll tax for workers
questions.explain: The law cut rates by about a quarter over three years and lowered the top rate on high incomes from 70 to 50 percent.

questions.q: What was a main feature of the Tax Reform Act of 1986?
options: It lowered rates while closing many deductions and loopholes
It raised the top individual rate to 70 percent to cut deficits
It created the first federal income tax on corporations
It abolished the IRS and shifted collection to the states
questions.explain: The law cut the top individual rate to 28 percent and reduced the number of tax brackets, a rare bipartisan change.

questions.q: In 1981 President Reagan fired striking members of which union?
options: The United Auto Workers union at Chrysler
The International Brotherhood of Teamsters
The United Mine Workers of America
The air traffic controllers' union PATCO
questions.explain: About 11,000 federal controllers who ignored a back-to-work order were dismissed, an episode often cited in debates over the decline of union power.

questions.q: During the 1980s the federal budget deficit and national debt did what?
options: Shrank steadily as new revenue and spending cuts produced surpluses
Fell to the lowest level in a century after the economic boom
Grew sharply as tax cuts were paired with higher defense spending
Stayed about the same because spending cuts offset lost revenue
questions.explain: Tax cuts and a defense buildup, along with weak revenue during the recession, produced large annual deficits, and the national debt more than doubled.

questions.q: Why did Congress pass the 1989 savings and loan bailout?
options: A stock market crash had wiped out most of the nation's brokerage firms
Hundreds of thrifts failed after deregulation and risky lending
A foreign government demanded repayment of loans made to American banks
Credit card companies defaulted after a collapse in consumer borrowing
questions.explain: Taxpayers covered much of the losses of failed thrifts, and the law created new regulators.

questions.q: Which group, founded in 1979 by Jerry Falwell, helped bring evangelical Christians into conservative politics?
options: The Eagle Forum
The Christian Coalition
The Federalist Society
The Moral Majority
questions.explain: It registered voters and lobbied against abortion and for traditional family values, and it helped Reagan in 1980.

questions.q: In 1981 President Reagan appointed which person as the first woman on the Supreme Court?
options: Ruth Bader Ginsburg
Jeane Kirkpatrick
Sandra Day O'Connor
Geraldine Ferraro
questions.explain: The Senate confirmed O'Connor, a former Arizona state judge, 99 to 0.

questions.q: Which event occurred outside the Washington Hilton on March 30, 1981?
options: A gunman wounded President Reagan in an assassination attempt
Reagan and Gorbachev signed an arms treaty at a summit dinner
A fire forced the evacuation of the president's staff at the hotel
Reagan delivered his farewell address to labor leaders
questions.explain: John Hinckley Jr. fired at the president, who recovered after surgery, and the incident raised his public standing.

questions.q: What did Reagan call the Soviet Union in a 1983 speech?
options: A paper tiger
An evil empire
A rogue state
An iron curtain
questions.explain: The speech to evangelicals reflected his hard-line view of communism, though he later negotiated with Moscow.

questions.q: What was the Strategic Defense Initiative announced by Reagan in 1983?
options: A new generation of land-based intercontinental nuclear missiles
A proposed missile defense system, nicknamed Star Wars
A treaty banning the deployment of weapons in space
A satellite network meant to improve weather forecasting
questions.explain: The plan imagined shielding the nation from nuclear attack with space-based weapons, and critics doubted it was feasible.

questions.q: What did the INF Treaty, signed by Reagan and Gorbachev in 1987, do?
options: Created a military alliance among Western European nations
Formally ended the Cold War between the two superpowers
Eliminated a class of intermediate-range nuclear missiles
Capped conventional troop levels in central Europe
questions.explain: The treaty was the first to remove an entire class of nuclear weapons, and both sides allowed inspections.

questions.q: Which Soviet leader introduced policies called glasnost and perestroika after taking power in 1985?
options: Leonid Brezhnev
Nikita Khrushchev
Boris Yeltsin
Mikhail Gorbachev
questions.explain: Glasnost meant openness and perestroika meant restructuring, and the reforms helped unleash forces that ended Soviet rule.

questions.q: At the Brandenburg Gate in 1987, Reagan challenged Gorbachev to do what?
options: Tear down the Berlin Wall
Address the U.S. Congress
Cut Soviet missile stocks
Withdraw from Afghanistan
questions.explain: The speech in West Berlin became one of the best known of his presidency.

questions.q: In what year did the Berlin Wall fall?
questions.explain: East Germany opened the border on November 9, 1989, and Germans began to dismantle the wall.

questions.q: The Soviet Union formally dissolved in what year?
questions.explain: Gorbachev resigned in December 1991, and the former republics became independent states, ending the Cold War rivalry.

questions.q: The START I treaty of 1991 was significant because it did what?
options: Cut the strategic nuclear arsenals of both superpowers
Established the United Nations arms inspection system
Banned all nuclear weapons held by either superpower
Limited antiballistic missile defenses in outer space
questions.explain: It was the first treaty to cut long-range nuclear arsenals rather than only cap them.

questions.q: Which events in Nicaragua did the Iran-Contra affair involve?
options: A U.S. military invasion meant to overthrow the ruling government
Secret aid to rebels fighting the government despite a congressional ban
A peace treaty between rebels and the government brokered by Congress
A trade agreement lifting sanctions in exchange for free elections
questions.explain: Officials sold arms to Iran and diverted profits to the Contras, and the Boland Amendment had barred such aid.

questions.q: When did the Iran-Contra affair become public?
options: August 1984
January 1991
October 1989
November 1986
questions.explain: After a Lebanese magazine reported the arms sales, investigators uncovered the diversion of funds.

questions.q: What was the effect of the 1983 bombing of the Marine barracks in Beirut?
options: It ended the Lebanese civil war and led to a Syrian withdrawal
It killed Lebanon's president and led to a U.S. invasion of Syria
It killed 241 U.S. service members and led to a U.S. withdrawal
It wounded 241 Marines but led to a larger U.S. troop deployment
questions.explain: The attack, one of the deadliest on Americans since Vietnam, preceded the removal of the Marines in 1984.

questions.q: In 1983 the United States invaded which Caribbean nation?
options: Barbados
Grenada
Trinidad
Jamaica
questions.explain: U.S. forces overthrew a Marxist government after a coup, and the action was popular at home but criticized abroad.

questions.q: In December 1989 President George H. W. Bush sent U.S. troops into which country?
options: Panama
Nicaragua
Colombia
Honduras
questions.explain: American forces removed General Manuel Noriega, who faced drug charges in the United States.

questions.q: What event led to the Persian Gulf War of 1990 and 1991?
options: Iraq's invasion of Kuwait
The Iranian revolution
The 1973 oil embargo
Syria's attack on Israel
questions.explain: Saddam Hussein's army took Kuwait in August 1990, and the UN Security Council demanded withdrawal.

questions.q: In January 1991, Congress took what action regarding the Gulf crisis?
options: It formally declared war on Iraq for the first time since 1941
It voted to reject military action and extend economic sanctions
It passed a trade embargo and froze all Iraqi assets in America
It authorized the use of military force to expel Iraq from Kuwait
questions.explain: The resolution passed narrowly, 52 to 47 in the Senate, before the air campaign began.

questions.q: What was the outcome of Operation Desert Storm in 1991?
options: A coalition occupied Baghdad and installed a new government
A stalemate along the Kuwaiti border that lasted for years
A coalition drove Iraq from Kuwait in a short war
A coalition overthrew Saddam Hussein within a hundred hours
questions.explain: After about a month of air strikes and a 100-hour ground war, Iraq withdrew and Saddam stayed in power.

questions.q: Which general chaired the Joint Chiefs of Staff during the Gulf War and was the first Black person in that role?
options: Tommy Franks
Colin Powell
Wesley Clark
Dick Cheney
questions.explain: Powell helped plan the war from the Pentagon, while Schwarzkopf commanded forces in the field.

questions.q: Which new technologies featured prominently in the Gulf War?
options: Precision-guided weapons, stealth aircraft, and satellite navigation
Atomic bombs, napalm, and defoliants of the kind used in Vietnam
Propeller bombers, wire-guided infantry radios, and signal balloons
Hydrogen bombs, trench artillery, and early radar warning posts
questions.explain: The war was seen as a showcase for modern air power and information systems.

questions.q: The Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 did what?
options: Created a federal health insurance program for disabled retirees
Banned disability discrimination and required public access
Required employers to meet hiring quotas for disabled workers
Created a pension system for workers injured on the job
questions.explain: Signed by President George H. W. Bush, it covered employment, public services, and transportation.

questions.q: The Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990 were notable for what?
options: Banning the sale of gasoline-powered passenger cars after 2000
Creating the Environmental Protection Agency as a federal body
Ending coal mining on federal land through a leasing ban
Creating a market-based system to cut acid rain emissions
questions.explain: The law allowed utilities to trade emission allowances, an approach later copied in other programs.

questions.q: Why was George H. W. Bush criticized by some conservatives in 1990?
options: He signed the Clean Water Act over strong industry objections
He vetoed the Gulf War resolution that Congress had approved
He agreed to a budget deal that included some tax increases
He proposed a national health insurance plan funded by payroll taxes
questions.explain: He had pledged "no new taxes" in 1988 but accepted a compromise to reduce the deficit.

questions.q: The Senate confirmed Clarence Thomas to the Supreme Court in 1991 after hearings featuring testimony from which person?
options: Janet Reno
Anita Hill
Gloria Allred
Paula Jones
questions.explain: Hill testified about alleged harassment, and Thomas denied the charges and was confirmed by a vote of 52 to 48.

questions.q: The 1992 Los Angeles riots followed which event?
options: The acquittal of police officers in the beating of Rodney King
The assassination of civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr.
The fatal police shooting of a teenager in the Watts district
The death of a rapper during a street confrontation in Compton
questions.explain: The verdict set off days of violence and led to debate about policing and race.

questions.q: Which independent candidate won about 19 percent of the popular vote in the 1992 presidential election?
options: Ralph Nader
John Anderson
Ross Perot
George Wallace
questions.explain: Perot ran as an independent focused on the deficit, and Bill Clinton won the presidency with 43 percent of the popular vote.

questions.q: The North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) linked the economies of which three countries?
options: The United States, Mexico, and Cuba
The United States, Canada, and Britain
The United States, Mexico, and Brazil
The United States, Canada, and Mexico
questions.explain: Congress approved it in 1993 and it took effect in 1994, ending most tariffs among the three.

questions.q: Which argument did critics of NAFTA make?
options: It would raise tariffs on Canadian goods
It would ban imports of Mexican farm goods
It could send manufacturing jobs to Mexico
It would reduce U.S. exports to Canada
questions.explain: Labor unions and others feared lower wages and plant closings, while supporters expected greater trade and lower prices.

questions.q: The "Don't Ask, Don't Tell" policy of 1993 did what?
options: Banned women from serving in combat units across all branches
Opened all military jobs to openly gay and lesbian service members
Required service members to take loyalty oaths about political groups
Allowed gay people to serve if they did not disclose their orientation
questions.explain: It was a compromise that barred open service, and discharges continued until its repeal in 2011.

questions.q: Which legislation signed by President Clinton in 1993 gave workers unpaid leave for family and medical needs?
options: The Family and Medical Leave Act
The Americans with Disabilities Act
The Fair Labor Standards Act
The Equal Pay Act
questions.explain: It guaranteed up to twelve weeks of leave for many workers without losing their jobs.

questions.q: What was the fate of President Clinton's 1993-94 health care reform plan?
options: It became law in 1994
It failed to pass Congress
It was approved by the Senate only
It was struck down by the Supreme Court
questions.explain: Led by Hillary Clinton, the effort faced opposition from insurers and Republicans and never came to a vote.

questions.q: The 1994 midterm elections were notable for what result?
options: Republicans won control of the House for the first time in forty years
Democrats expanded their House majority to the largest in decades
Ross Perot's Reform Party won a majority of Senate seats
A third party won enough seats to control the House of Representatives
questions.explain: Newt Gingrich and the "Contract with America" helped bring the party to power in Congress.

questions.q: Why did parts of the federal government shut down in late 1995 and early 1996?
options: A hurricane struck Washington and closed federal offices for weeks
A court ordered agencies to close during an ethics investigation
Federal workers went on strike over pay and pension disputes
Clinton and Republicans in Congress disagreed over the budget
questions.explain: The longest shutdown to that point came after the two sides could not agree on spending priorities.

questions.q: What did the 1996 welfare reform law do?
options: Expanded AFDC benefits and removed work requirements for recipients
Ended the AFDC entitlement and set work requirements and time limits
Banned the food stamp program and replaced it with state grants
Created Medicare coverage for low-income single mothers and children
questions.explain: It created Temporary Assistance for Needy Families and was signed by Clinton after two vetoes of earlier versions.

questions.q: The Defense of Marriage Act of 1996 defined marriage for federal purposes as what?
options: A civil contract between any two adults
A religious sacrament recognized only by churches
A union between one man and one woman
A matter left entirely for each state to define
questions.explain: The law also said states need not recognize same-sex marriages from other states, and a key section was later struck down in United States v. Windsor.

questions.q: The Telecommunications Act of 1996 did what?
options: Created the Federal Communications Commission as a new agency
Rewrote communications law to open markets to competition
Banned cable television in markets with broadcast stations
Required licenses for the first commercial radio stations
questions.explain: It was the first major overhaul in decades and included rules for new technology.

questions.q: The 1995 Oklahoma City bombing killed 168 people. At what building did it occur?
options: A university campus
An Army recruiting depot
A county courthouse
A federal office building
questions.explain: Timothy McVeigh set off a truck bomb at the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building. It remains the deadliest act of domestic terrorism in U.S. history.

questions.q: The 1995 Dayton Accords ended the war in which place?
options: Kosovo
Croatia
Bosnia
Slovenia
questions.explain: The agreement, brokered by the United States, split Bosnia into two entities and brought in NATO peacekeepers.

questions.q: In 1999 NATO conducted an air campaign against Yugoslavia over which issue?
options: Treatment of ethnic Albanians in Kosovo
A border dispute between Serbia and Albania
Serbian attacks on Bosnian Muslim towns
Yugoslav seizure of disputed Croatian territory
questions.explain: The bombing lasted about eleven weeks and ended with Yugoslav forces leaving Kosovo.

questions.q: The House of Representatives impeached President Bill Clinton in what year?
questions.explain: The House approved articles in December 1998, and the Senate acquitted him in February 1999.

questions.q: What were the charges in the House's articles of impeachment against Clinton?
options: Treason and accepting illegal foreign gifts
Tax evasion and campaign finance fraud
Perjury and obstruction of justice
Bribery and misuse of federal funds
questions.explain: The charges grew out of his testimony about a relationship with a White House intern in a lawsuit and a grand jury.

questions.q: What was the outcome of the Senate trial of President Clinton in 1999?
options: He was convicted of perjury but kept his office
He was removed from office by a two-thirds vote
He resigned before the Senate could hold a vote
He was acquitted on both articles of impeachment
questions.explain: The Senate did not reach the two-thirds needed on either charge, and Chief Justice William Rehnquist presided.

questions.q: Who presides over a presidential impeachment trial in the Senate?
options: The Speaker of the House of Representatives
The Chief Justice of the United States
The President pro tempore of the Senate
The Attorney General of the United States
questions.explain: The Constitution assigns the role to the Chief Justice, and in 1999 it was William Rehnquist.

questions.q: How many presidents have been impeached by the House before the end of the 1990s?
options: One
Three
Two
None
questions.explain: Andrew Johnson was impeached in 1868 and Bill Clinton in 1998, and both were acquitted by the Senate.

questions.q: What happened to the federal budget at the end of the 1990s?
options: Deficits widened sharply in every year of the decade
The federal government recorded budget surpluses
The national debt was completely paid off by 2000
Deficits doubled during a sharp recession in 1998
questions.explain: Rising revenues from the economic expansion, along with budget deals, produced surpluses from 1998 to 2001.

questions.q: In 2000 Congress granted China permanent normal trade relations, which prepared China to do what?
options: Join the World Trade Organization
Adopt a currency tied to the dollar
Join the G7 group of industrial nations
Join the North Atlantic alliance
questions.explain: China entered the WTO in 2001, and trade between the two nations grew sharply.

questions.q: The World Wide Web was invented by whom?
options: Marc Andreessen
Steve Wozniak
Robert Metcalfe
Tim Berners-Lee
questions.explain: Berners-Lee developed it at CERN in 1989 and 1990 as a way to share documents over the internet.

questions.q: What was the importance of the Mosaic browser in 1993?
options: It made the web easy for ordinary users
It sent the first email between universities
It launched the first commercial search engine
It started the internet as a research network
questions.explain: Its graphical design helped the internet spread beyond universities and research labs.

questions.q: The "dot-com bubble" of the late 1990s refers to what?
options: A real estate boom and bust in technology office parks
A rapid rise and crash in internet company stock prices
A new federal tax on commerce conducted through websites
A nationwide breakdown of the telephone network in 1999
questions.explain: Many internet start-ups lost value in 2000 and 2001 after investors realized profits were uncertain.

questions.q: Which device introduced by Apple in 2007 helped popularize smartphones?
options: The iPod
The Macintosh
The iPhone
The Newton
questions.explain: It combined a phone, a music player, and an internet browser with a touch screen.

questions.q: Which 1981 product from IBM helped make personal computers common in offices and homes?
options: The Altair
The Apple II
The Macintosh
The IBM PC
questions.explain: The open design led many companies to produce compatible machines, and Microsoft supplied the operating system.

questions.q: The Library of Congress launched which online service in 1995 to give the public access to bills and legislative information?
options: PACER
ARPANET
Westlaw
THOMAS
questions.explain: It was later replaced by Congress.gov and showed how Congress began to use the web.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the Copyright Office, which is part of the Library of Congress?
options: To examine and grant patents for inventions
To register works and record copyright claims
To fund publication of books by new authors
To print currency and engrave postage stamps
questions.explain: Copyright registration is handled there, and copies of many registered works have historically been deposited with the Library.

questions.q: The Copyright Act of 1976, effective in 1978, did what?
options: Set the framework for modern U.S. copyright and extended terms
Established the first U.S. patent system under the Constitution
Abolished copyright protection for works made by corporations
Required formal registration before any copyright protection existed
questions.explain: The law gave works automatic protection from creation, with terms based on the life of the author.

questions.q: What happened to the space shuttle Challenger on January 28, 1986?
options: It landed safely after its mission was cut short by engine trouble
It exploded on the launch pad during a routine countdown rehearsal
It broke apart shortly after liftoff, killing all seven crew members
It was lost in orbit after a collision with a piece of space debris
questions.explain: The disaster, watched live by many schoolchildren, grounded the shuttle fleet for almost three years.

questions.q: What did the Rogers Commission conclude about the Challenger disaster?
options: Crew error during ascent caused loss of control of the orbiter
Debris from an orbiting satellite struck the shuttle after liftoff
Sabotage of the fuel system caused the explosion shortly after launch
A booster O-ring failed in cold weather and managers had not acted on engineers' warnings
questions.explain: The commission found that a booster seal failed in cold weather and that engineers' concerns about the low temperature were not acted on.

questions.q: Who was Christa McAuliffe, who died aboard Challenger?
options: The mission commander who led the Challenger flight crew
A Navy test pilot selected as the shuttle's flight engineer
A teacher chosen to be the first private citizen in space
A NASA physicist who designed the shuttle's heat tiles
questions.explain: Her selection through the Teacher in Space project drew large audiences of students for the launch.

questions.q: Who became the first American woman in space, in 1983?
options: Christa McAuliffe
Sally Ride
Eileen Collins
Mae Jemison
questions.explain: Ride flew aboard Challenger as a mission specialist, and she later served on the investigations of both shuttle disasters.

questions.q: The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, needed a repair mission in 1993 to fix what problem?
options: A flaw in its main mirror
A jammed communications antenna
A cracked fuel storage tank
A damaged solar panel array
questions.explain: Astronauts installed corrective optics in 1993, and Hubble went on to produce important images and data.

questions.q: What was the International Space Station, begun in 1998?
options: An orbiting laboratory built by the U.S., Russia, and partners
A Soviet military space station taken over by NATO members
A permanent lunar settlement built by NASA and private firms
A U.S. Navy platform for tracking enemy submarines from space
questions.explain: The partnership signaled post-Cold War cooperation, and the station has had crews on board continuously since November 2000.

questions.q: The space shuttle Columbia was lost in what year?
questions.explain: The shuttle broke up while returning to Earth on February 1, 2003, after foam damaged its wing during launch.

questions.q: The space shuttle program ended in what year?
questions.explain: After 135 missions, Atlantis made the last flight in July 2011, and astronauts then traveled on Russian craft until commercial vehicles were ready.

questions.q: What is the Global Positioning System (GPS)?
options: A cellular phone network developed by a consortium of carriers
A civilian weather radar network run by the Commerce Department
A satellite television service launched by commercial broadcasters
A military-built satellite navigation system later opened to civilians
questions.explain: It began as a Defense Department project and became widely used for maps, timing, and aviation.

questions.q: How did satellites change the Cold War?
options: They replaced intercontinental missiles with orbiting weapons platforms
They allowed superpowers to monitor each other's arms and verify treaties
They ended the space race by merging U.S. and Soviet programs
They gave the military no use beyond weather and communications
questions.explain: Reconnaissance satellites gave leaders confidence to sign arms limits since compliance could be checked from space.

questions.q: The Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986 did what?
options: Legalized many unauthorized immigrants and penalized employers who hired them
Ended family-based visas and set a points system for skilled workers worldwide
Created the national origins quota system and a new federal border police force
Banned immigration from Latin America and deported many recent arrivals
questions.explain: About three million people gained legal status, but the employer sanctions were weakly enforced.

questions.q: The Immigration Act of 1990 did what?
options: Lowered annual limits on legal immigration and ended family visas
Ended asylum protections for refugees and created a guest-worker visa
Raised the annual cap on legal immigration and created a diversity visa
Created the DACA program for young unauthorized immigrants
questions.explain: Signed by George H. W. Bush, the Immigration Act of 1990 raised the annual cap on legal immigration, expanded visas for skilled workers and families, and created the diversity visa lottery.

questions.q: California's 1994 Proposition 187 attempted to do what?
options: Make English the state's only official language
Grant citizenship to the children of immigrants
Limit legal immigration from Mexico and Asia
Deny public services to unauthorized immigrants
questions.explain: Voters approved it, but federal courts blocked most of it as an intrusion on federal authority over immigration.

questions.q: The Census Bureau reported that by the early 2000s which group had become the nation's largest minority?
options: African Americans
Asian Americans
Hispanic Americans
Native Americans
questions.explain: Immigration and high birth rates since 1965 had raised the Hispanic population, a change in the nation's demographics.

questions.q: DACA, announced by the Obama administration in 2012, did what?
options: Gave some people brought here as children temporary protection from deportation
Granted citizenship to people brought here as children who enlisted in the military
Suspended new immigration from several countries during a national emergency
Created a seasonal guest-worker program for agricultural employers
questions.explain: The executive action offered renewable two-year permits to eligible young unauthorized immigrants, though Congress did not pass a law on it.

questions.q: The Secure Fence Act of 2006 authorized what?
options: Construction of a wall along the U.S.-Canada border
Construction of barriers along parts of the U.S.-Mexico border
Creation of a cabinet department for border and port security
A path to citizenship for unauthorized workers in agriculture
questions.explain: It reflected rising political concern about unauthorized immigration, and fencing was built on hundreds of miles of border.

questions.q: The 1981 discovery of unusual cases of immune system failure marked the start of what public health crisis?
options: The polio epidemic
The influenza pandemic
The AIDS epidemic
The measles outbreak
questions.explain: Reported in 1981, the disease led to thousands of deaths by the late 1980s and prompted debate over research funding.

questions.q: What was MTV, launched in 1981, an example of?
options: A federal agency that set licensing rules for radio stations
A cable channel centered on music videos that shaped youth culture
A radio network that broadcast live concerts nationwide
A film studio that produced concert movies for theaters
questions.explain: The channel helped make video a central part of the music industry.

questions.q: Which Supreme Court decision of December 2000 effectively ended the Florida recount in the presidential election?
options: Baker v. Carr
Buckley v. Valeo
United States v. Nixon
Bush v. Gore
questions.explain: The Court ruled that the recount procedures raised equal protection problems and that there was no time to fix them, and George W. Bush won Florida.

questions.q: In the 2000 presidential election, which unusual result occurred?
options: Al Gore won the popular vote while George W. Bush won the Electoral College
Ralph Nader carried several Western states and denied both major candidates a majority
The House of Representatives decided the winner after the Electoral College tied
George W. Bush won the popular vote while Al Gore won the Electoral College
questions.explain: Bush received 271 electoral votes to Gore's 266, with Florida's margin of a few hundred votes deciding the result.

questions.q: What was the Court's equal protection reasoning in Bush v. Gore?
