options: Florida's legislature had no power to set rules for counting ballots
Many ballots had been lost or destroyed by county election officials
Different counties were using different standards to count ballots
Voters in several counties had been intimidated at polling places
questions.explain: The justices said that unequal standards for counting violated the 14th Amendment, and a majority said time had run out.

questions.q: How many airliners were hijacked in the attacks of September 11, 2001?
options: Two
Six
Nine
Four
questions.explain: Two hit the World Trade Center towers, one hit the Pentagon, and one crashed in a field in Pennsylvania.

questions.q: At which location did American Airlines Flight 77 crash on September 11, 2001?
options: The Pentagon
The White House
The Capitol
The World Trade Center
questions.explain: The crash killed 184 people, including those on the plane and in the building.

questions.q: What happened to United Flight 93 on September 11, 2001?
options: It struck the Capitol building after hijackers overpowered the flight crew and passengers
It crashed in Pennsylvania after passengers tried to take control from the hijackers
It was shot down over Ohio by military fighter jets sent from Andrews Air Force Base
It hit the Pentagon's west side after circling over Washington, D.C. for an hour
questions.explain: Passengers learned about the other attacks and fought back, and the plane went down near Shanksville.

questions.q: Which terrorist group carried out the September 11 attacks?
options: The Taliban
Al-Qaeda
Hezbollah
Hamas
questions.explain: Osama bin Laden's network trained and financed nineteen hijackers.

questions.q: How many people were killed in the September 11 attacks, not counting the hijackers?
options: About 3,000
About 300
About 30,000
About 1,000
questions.explain: The number of victims was nearly 3,000, including civilians, first responders, and military personnel.

questions.q: When did the Pentagon Memorial, with 184 benches, open to the public?
questions.explain: It stands near the site where the plane struck, and each bench honors a person who died.

questions.q: What did the Authorization for Use of Military Force, passed by Congress on September 14, 2001, allow?
options: A formal declaration of war against Afghanistan and the Taliban government
The creation of a cabinet department to coordinate domestic security
Indefinite detention of U.S. citizens suspected of ties to terrorism
The president to use force against those responsible for the attacks
questions.explain: Congress passed it almost unanimously, and it has been cited as legal basis for many operations.

questions.q: Which law signed in October 2001 expanded the government's surveillance powers to fight terrorism?
options: The Espionage Act
The Smith Act
The Alien and Sedition Acts
The USA PATRIOT Act
questions.explain: Passed six weeks after the attacks, it broadened sharing of information among agencies and increased powers for searches and wiretaps.

questions.q: What was a criticism of the Patriot Act raised by civil liberties groups?
options: It required all citizens to carry national identification cards
Some provisions could infringe on privacy and the Fourth Amendment
It reinstated a military draft for young men to fight terrorism
It gave the president power to suspend Congress during emergencies
questions.explain: Critics argued that powers to collect records and use roving wiretaps could reach law-abiding people, and Congress added sunset dates to some parts.

questions.q: By what margin did the Senate pass the Patriot Act in October 2001?
options: 98 to 1
questions.explain: Russ Feingold cast the only no vote, and the House approved the bill by a wide margin as well.

questions.q: Which department was created by Congress in 2002 to coordinate efforts against terrorism at home?
options: The Department of Veterans Affairs
The Department of National Intelligence
The Department of Homeland Security
The Department of the Treasury
questions.explain: It combined about two dozen agencies, such as the Coast Guard and the Secret Service, into a new cabinet department.

questions.q: Which agency was created in late 2001 to take over security at airports?
options: The Transportation Security Administration
The Federal Aviation Administration
The Federal Bureau of Investigation
The Immigration and Naturalization Service
questions.explain: Federal officers replaced private screeners after the attacks.

questions.q: The National Commission on Terrorist Attacks Upon the United States, known as the 9/11 Commission, reported in 2004 that what?
options: Iraq had provided direct operational support to the hijackers' plot
The attacks were unavoidable given the limits of existing technology
The FBI alone was responsible for missing warnings before the attacks
Agencies had failed to share information and recommended reforms
questions.explain: The bipartisan panel recommended a Director of National Intelligence and better coordination.

questions.q: U.S. forces launched military operations in Afghanistan in October 2001 to do what?
options: Support the Taliban in a war against Iranian-backed militias
Remove the Taliban government that sheltered al-Qaeda
Defend Pakistan against an Indian invasion across Kashmir
Destroy Iranian nuclear facilities near the Afghan border
questions.explain: The Taliban fell within weeks, but the war lasted twenty years.

questions.q: In May 2011, U.S. Navy SEALs killed which leader in a raid in Pakistan?
options: Saddam Hussein
Muammar Gaddafi
Osama bin Laden
Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi
questions.explain: President Obama announced that the al-Qaeda leader was dead after the operation in Abbottabad.

questions.q: When were the last U.S. troops withdrawn from Afghanistan?
options: December 2011
May 2003
January 2009
August 2021
questions.explain: The withdrawal, completed at the end of August 2021, followed an agreement made in 2020 and ended the longest war in American history.

questions.q: Which section of Arlington National Cemetery is known for graves of those killed in Iraq and Afghanistan?
options: Section 1
Section 60
Section 27
Section 9
questions.explain: Many families visit the section, which became a burial place for casualties of the wars after 2001.

questions.q: In Boumediene v. Bush (2008), the Supreme Court ruled that detainees at Guantanamo Bay had what right?
options: The right to a jury trial in a civilian federal court
The right to immediate release and compensation for detention
The right to challenge their detention in federal court
The right to a speedy trial before a military tribunal
questions.explain: The Court held that the Constitution's habeas corpus protection extended to the detainees.

questions.q: What was the main justification used by the Bush administration for the 2003 invasion of Iraq?
options: The claim that Iraq had weapons of mass destruction
A request for assistance from the new Iraqi parliament
Iraqi attacks on American warships in the Persian Gulf
A treaty obligation to defend Kuwait against a renewed attack
questions.explain: Officials said Iraq had banned weapons programs, but no stockpiles were found after the invasion.

questions.q: In October 2002, Congress passed a resolution that did what?
options: Formally declared war on Iraq under the Constitution
Placed economic sanctions on Iraq until weapons inspectors returned
Approved funding for reconstruction of Iraq after the invasion
Authorized the president to use force against Iraq
questions.explain: The House and Senate approved it by large margins before the invasion in March 2003.

questions.q: What happened after U.S. forces took Baghdad in April 2003?
options: A peace treaty ended the war and troops left within months
A stable democracy emerged quickly and troops left that summer
An insurgency developed and U.S. troops stayed for years
Saddam Hussein regained power with Iranian military support
questions.explain: Large-scale fighting between Iraqis and the coalition lasted for years, and American forces left in December 2011.

questions.q: The "surge" announced in 2007 referred to what?
options: A surge in domestic oil production
An increase in U.S. troops in Iraq
A campaign to register military voters
A series of hurricanes on the Gulf Coast
questions.explain: President Bush sent additional troops to improve security in Baghdad and Anbar province.

questions.q: Photographs from Abu Ghraib prison in 2004 caused controversy because they showed what?
options: Abuse of detainees by U.S. personnel
A bombing of a hospital by U.S. aircraft
A prisoner exchange with Iraqi insurgents
A battle in Fallujah involving U.S. Marines
questions.explain: The images led to investigations and damaged the American image abroad.

questions.q: When did the last U.S. troops leave Iraq under a 2008 agreement between the two countries?
options: October 2008
February 2009
August 2003
December 2011
questions.explain: The agreement signed in 2008 set the date, and the last troops left at the end of 2011.

questions.q: The No Child Left Behind Act of 2002 required states to do what?
options: Replace state testing with a single national curriculum
Test students in reading and math and report results
Provide free tuition at community colleges for all students
Close the Department of Education and transfer its duties
questions.explain: The law tied federal funding to testing and made schools accountable for the progress of student groups.

questions.q: The Medicare Modernization Act of 2003 added which benefit?
options: Dental and vision coverage for seniors
Health coverage for low-income children
Prescription drug coverage for seniors
Long-term nursing home care for veterans
questions.explain: The Part D program began in 2006 and was one of the largest expansions of Medicare since its creation.

questions.q: The Bush tax cuts of 2001 and 2003 did what?
options: Reduced income tax rates and taxes on dividends and capital gains
Raised the top income tax rate while expanding the earned income credit
Replaced the income tax with a flat national consumption tax
Created a federal sales tax to pay for the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq
questions.explain: Supporters said they would help growth, while critics said they increased deficits and favored high earners.

questions.q: Hurricane Katrina struck the Gulf Coast in August 2005. Which city was largely flooded after levees failed?
options: New Orleans
Baton Rouge
Galveston
Mobile, Alabama
questions.explain: The storm killed more than a thousand people, and the federal response was widely criticized.

questions.q: In District of Columbia v. Heller (2008), the Supreme Court held what about the Second Amendment?
options: It protects the right to bear arms only for service in state militias
It allows cities to ban handguns in homes when public safety requires
It protects an individual right to keep firearms for self-defense in the home
It forbids any federal or state regulation of firearms ownership and sales
questions.explain: The 5-4 decision struck down a Washington, D.C., ban on handguns in homes, while saying some regulations remain valid.

questions.q: In Lawrence v. Texas (2003), the Supreme Court did what?
options: Upheld a state ban on abortion after the first trimester of pregnancy
Upheld Georgia's sodomy law as a valid exercise of state police power
Legalized same-sex marriage in all fifty states under equal protection
Struck down state laws that criminalized private same-sex conduct
questions.explain: The ruling overturned an earlier decision, Bowers v. Hardwick, and later cases built on its reasoning.

questions.q: In Grutter v. Bollinger (2003), the Supreme Court allowed what?
options: Fixed racial quotas in law school admissions to ensure diversity
Using race as one factor in law school admissions to promote diversity
A ban on any consideration of race in public university admissions
Racial preferences in public hiring to remedy past discrimination
questions.explain: The majority said student diversity was a compelling interest if race was considered in a flexible, individualized way.

questions.q: In Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023), the Supreme Court ruled what?
options: Race could still be used as a plus factor at both universities, with new limits
Colleges had to adopt racial quotas to remedy past discrimination in admissions
Race-conscious admissions at Harvard and North Carolina violated equal protection
Public colleges could keep using race in admissions but private ones could not
questions.explain: The Court ruled 6-3 against North Carolina and 6-2 against Harvard, holding both programs violated equal protection; Justice Jackson did not take part in the Harvard case.

questions.q: In Texas v. Johnson (1989), the Supreme Court ruled that what?
options: States could ban flag burning to preserve the flag as a national symbol
Burning the American flag as political protest was protected speech
Public school students could be required to salute the flag each day
Flags could be removed from public school classrooms and buildings
questions.explain: The 5-4 decision said that the government cannot prohibit expression because society finds it offensive.

questions.q: In Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992), the Supreme Court did what?
options: Overturned Roe v. Wade entirely and allowed states to ban abortion at any stage
Reaffirmed Roe v. Wade and barred states from any regulation such as waiting periods
Held that Congress could ban abortion nationwide under the Commerce Clause
Reaffirmed Roe v. Wade's core but allowed more state regulation under an undue-burden test
questions.explain: The plurality opinion kept a constitutional right to abortion before viability but let states regulate if they did not impose an undue burden.

questions.q: What was a major cause of the financial crisis that began in 2007?
options: Lenders made many risky subprime mortgages that were bundled into securities
A sudden collapse in oil prices that bankrupted major energy producers worldwide
A war in the Middle East that sharply disrupted global shipping and oil trade
A nationwide banking holiday that froze deposits at the largest American banks
questions.explain: When housing prices fell, borrowers defaulted and investors who held mortgage-backed securities suffered large losses.

questions.q: Which large investment bank's bankruptcy in September 2008 deepened the financial panic?
options: Goldman Sachs
Lehman Brothers
Bear Stearns
JPMorgan Chase
questions.explain: The failure of the firm, with no federal rescue, froze credit markets and contributed to stock market declines.

questions.q: What was the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP), passed in October 2008?
options: A $700 billion program to stabilize financial institutions
A $700 billion stimulus for road and bridge building
A temporary tax cut for middle-income families and retirees
A law forgiving mortgage debt for homeowners facing foreclosure
questions.explain: The Treasury used the funds to inject capital into banks, aid automakers, and support housing programs, and most of it was repaid.

questions.q: The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 did what?
options: Created a new agency to regulate mortgage lenders and consumer credit
Banned mergers among the largest banks to prevent future bailouts
Eliminated the mortgage interest deduction to finance deficit reduction
Provided about $787 billion in tax cuts and spending to boost the economy
questions.explain: Passed early in the Obama administration, it included aid to states, infrastructure, and unemployment benefits.

questions.q: What did the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 create?
options: The Federal Reserve System to supervise the nation's largest banks
The Securities and Exchange Commission to police stock markets
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and new rules for banks
The FDIC to insure customer deposits at member banks
questions.explain: It was the largest overhaul of financial regulation since the 1930s and followed the 2008 crisis.

questions.q: At what level did the U.S. unemployment rate peak during the Great Recession?
options: About 10 percent
About 5 percent
About 15 percent
About 20 percent
questions.explain: Unemployment reached 10 percent in late 2009, and recovery in jobs was slow.

questions.q: During the Great Recession, which institution cut its main interest rate nearly to zero?
options: The Treasury Department
The Export-Import Bank
The Commerce Department
The Federal Reserve
questions.explain: The central bank also bought large amounts of bonds to ease credit.

questions.q: Who won the 2008 presidential election to become the first African American president?
options: Jesse Jackson
Barack Obama
Colin Powell
Al Sharpton
questions.explain: Obama defeated John McCain, and he took office in January 2009.

questions.q: In 2009 Sonia Sotomayor became which Supreme Court justice?
options: The first female justice
The first Black justice
The first Hispanic justice
The first Asian American
questions.explain: Obama nominated her, and the Senate confirmed her on a vote of 68 to 31.

questions.q: Which justice, confirmed in 2022, was the first Black woman on the Supreme Court?
options: Sonia Maria Sotomayor
Ketanji Brown Jackson
Ruth Bader Ginsburg
Anthony McLeod Kennedy
questions.explain: Ketanji Brown Jackson, nominated by President Biden, was confirmed in 2022 as the first Black woman on the Supreme Court. She succeeded Justice Stephen Breyer.

questions.q: The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act was signed into law in what year?
questions.explain: President Obama signed it in March 2010 after months of debate in Congress.

questions.q: Which provision was part of the Affordable Care Act?
options: Young adults could stay on a parent's plan until age 26
The federal government took over management of all hospitals
Medicare was replaced by a single-payer system for all ages
Employers were forbidden from offering private health insurance
questions.explain: The law also barred insurers from denying coverage for pre-existing conditions and created health insurance marketplaces.

questions.q: In National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius (2012), the Supreme Court did what?
options: Struck down the individual mandate and left the rest of the law intact
Upheld the entire law as a valid use of the Commerce Clause power
Upheld the individual mandate as a tax and limited the Medicaid expansion
Struck down the entire law because Congress lacks power over health care
questions.explain: Chief Justice Roberts wrote that the penalty was a valid use of the taxing power, though states could not be forced to expand Medicaid.

questions.q: Which Senate procedure was important in the passage of the ACA in December 2009?
options: A two-thirds vote to override a presidential veto
A Supreme Court ruling on its constitutionality
A national referendum on health care reform
The Senate had to find 60 votes to end debate
questions.explain: Democrats and the two independents who caucused with them held exactly 60 seats, enough to overcome a Republican filibuster.

questions.q: The Don't Ask, Don't Tell policy was repealed in 2010 by which action?
options: A ruling by the Supreme Court
A law signed by President Obama
An order from the Joint Chiefs
A referendum held in the states
questions.explain: The repeal took effect in 2011 and allowed gay and lesbian service members to serve openly.

questions.q: In Obergefell v. Hodges (2015), the Supreme Court ruled what?
options: States could choose whether to recognize same-sex marriages
Marriage regulation belonged only to the federal government
States must license and recognize same-sex marriages
Religious groups had to perform same-sex marriages on request
questions.explain: The 5-4 decision held that the 14th Amendment guarantees the right to marry to same-sex couples.

questions.q: In United States v. Windsor (2013), the Court struck down part of which law?
options: The Defense of Marriage Act
The Voting Rights Act of 1965
The Matthew Shepard Act
The Affordable Care Act
questions.explain: The Court held that the federal definition of marriage that excluded same-sex couples violated the Fifth Amendment.

questions.q: In Citizens United v. FEC (2010), the Supreme Court held what about political spending?
options: Corporations could donate directly to candidates and parties without any legal limit
All limits on contributions to candidates and parties violate the First Amendment
Foreign corporations and governments may spend freely in United States elections
The government cannot ban independent political spending by corporations and unions
questions.explain: The 5-4 ruling held on First Amendment grounds that independent expenditures cannot be limited based on the speaker's corporate identity.

questions.q: Citizens United helped lead to the growth of what kind of organization?
options: Labor unions
Political parties
Super PACs
Think tanks
questions.explain: Groups that raised unlimited sums for independent advertising became important after the decision and a related appeals court case.

questions.q: The Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002 is also known by which name?
options: Taft-Hartley Act
McCain-Feingold
Dodd-Frank Act
Humphrey-Hawkins
questions.explain: The law banned unregulated "soft money" contributions to national parties, and parts were later limited by the Supreme Court.

questions.q: Which movements of 2009 and 2011 reflected public anger after the financial crisis?
options: The Tea Party and Occupy Wall Street
The Progressive and Populist parties
The New Left and the John Birch Society
The Moral Majority and the Black Panthers
questions.explain: The Tea Party called for lower taxes and smaller government, while Occupy protesters criticized economic inequality.

questions.q: Which term describes the increasing ideological distance between the two major parties in Congress since the 1970s?
options: Realignment
Polarization
Dealignment
Bipartisanship
questions.explain: Voting records show fewer moderates in each party, and cooperation across party lines has declined.

questions.q: Who won the Electoral College in the 2016 presidential election?
options: Donald Trump
Hillary Clinton
Bernie Sanders
Mitt Romney
questions.explain: Trump won 304 electoral votes, while Clinton received about 2.9 million more popular votes nationwide.

questions.q: Who became the first woman elected vice president when she won in 2020?
options: Geraldine Ferraro
Sarah Palin
Hillary Clinton
Kamala Harris
questions.explain: Harris was also the first Black and first South Asian American vice president, serving with President Joe Biden.

questions.q: In the 2020 presidential election, which candidate won the presidency?
options: Donald Trump
Bernie Sanders
Joe Biden
Mike Pence
questions.explain: Biden won 306 electoral votes and took office on January 20, 2021.

questions.q: Who won the 2024 presidential election?
options: Donald Trump
Joe Biden
Kamala Harris
Nikki Haley
questions.explain: Trump defeated Vice President Harris, winning 312 electoral votes, and took office in January 2025.

questions.q: Which president was impeached twice by the House of Representatives?
options: Bill Clinton
Andrew Johnson
Richard Nixon
Donald Trump
questions.explain: The House impeached him in December 2019 and again in January 2021, and the Senate voted to acquit in both trials.

questions.q: What was the outcome of the Senate trial of President Trump in February 2020?
options: He was convicted
He was acquitted
He was censured
He was removed
questions.explain: The Senate voted on two articles and did not reach the two-thirds needed for conviction.

questions.q: On January 6, 2021, what interrupted Congress's joint session to count electoral votes?
options: A fire that broke out in the Rotunda
A power failure across the Capitol
A crowd entered the Capitol building
A severe snowstorm over Washington
questions.explain: The session resumed that night, and Congress completed the count and certified the result in the early morning hours of January 7.

questions.q: What body must approve an impeachment of the president before a Senate trial can occur?
options: The Senate Judiciary Committee
The House of Representatives
The Supreme Court justices
A majority of the cabinet
questions.explain: The House has the sole power to impeach, and the Senate has the sole power to try impeachments.

questions.q: What did the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act of March 2020 provide?
options: A nationwide lockdown order enforced by federal agencies for a month
A ban on all international travel to and from the United States
About $2.2 trillion in aid for households, businesses, and hospitals
A new payroll tax to fund pandemic vaccines and testing
questions.explain: The law sent payments to many households, expanded unemployment benefits, and provided loans to small businesses.

questions.q: In March 2020, what did the World Health Organization declare about COVID-19?
options: That it was a minor outbreak
That it was contained
That it had a vaccine
That it was a pandemic
questions.explain: The declaration on March 11, 2020, came as cases spread across continents, and the U.S. declared a national emergency days later.

questions.q: When did the first COVID-19 vaccine receive emergency use authorization in the United States?
options: December 2020
March 2019
June 2021
September 2022
questions.explain: The FDA authorized the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine on December 11, 2020, followed by a second vaccine a week later.

questions.q: What happened to U.S. unemployment in the spring of 2020?
options: It stayed below 4 percent as federal aid protected workers' jobs
It rose to levels not seen since the Great Depression
It fell to a record low as remote work jobs expanded
It held steady near pre-pandemic levels throughout the spring
questions.explain: The rate reached about 14.8 percent in April 2020 (first reported as 14.7 percent) as businesses closed to slow the spread of the virus.

questions.q: In Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022), the Supreme Court ruled what?
options: The Constitution confers no right to abortion and the issue returns to the states
Roe v. Wade was reaffirmed and the viability standard was left in place
States must allow abortion until fetal viability under the Constitution's privacy guarantee
Congress alone has power to set a national limit on abortion procedures
questions.explain: The decision overruled Roe v. Wade and Planned Parenthood v. Casey and allowed states to regulate abortion.

questions.q: The Dobbs case concerned a Mississippi law that did what?
options: Banned all abortions except to save the life of the mother
Required parental consent for every minor seeking an abortion
Banned most abortions after fifteen weeks of pregnancy
Created a mandatory waiting period and counseling requirement
questions.explain: The state asked the Court to uphold the law, and the justices did so, overruling earlier precedents.

questions.q: Which justice wrote the majority opinion in Dobbs?
options: John Roberts
Stephen Breyer
Clarence Thomas
Samuel Alito
questions.explain: The opinion was issued on June 24, 2022, and Chief Justice Roberts concurred in the judgment only.

questions.q: Who became Chief Justice of the United States in 2005?
options: William Rehnquist
Samuel Alito
John Roberts
Antonin Scalia
questions.explain: Roberts succeeded William Rehnquist, who died in office, and had been nominated by George W. Bush.

questions.q: The growth of social media in the 2000s began with platforms like which one launched in 2004?
options: Instagram
Facebook
TikTok
Snapchat
questions.explain: Mark Zuckerberg launched it at Harvard, and it spread to the public in 2006.

questions.q: What does the term "globalization" describe in the late twentieth century?
options: A policy of limiting foreign trade to protect industries and local workers
A shift toward self-sufficient local economies and regional trade barriers
The creation of a single world government to regulate trade and migration
The growing integration of economies, trade, and communication across the world
questions.explain: Lower tariffs, container shipping, and the internet linked markets and raised both trade and debates about jobs.

questions.q: What is "deindustrialization," often used to describe parts of the Midwest?
options: The decline of manufacturing jobs and factories
The rapid expansion of steel mills and auto plants
A boom in new factories built in Rust Belt cities
A shift of Midwestern workers from factories to farming
questions.explain: Plant closings and automation in the 1970s and later led to job losses in cities like Detroit and Youngstown.

questions.q: The Korean War Veterans Memorial in Washington was dedicated in 1995. Which phrase is carved on its granite wall?
options: Freedom Is Not Free
Duty, Honor, Country
Peace Through Strength
Remember the Forgotten Soldier
questions.explain: The wall also bears etched faces from archival photographs, and nineteen statues of soldiers on patrol move through the memorial's field.

questions.q: What is the main sculptural feature of the Korean War Veterans Memorial?
options: A single bronze statue of a general standing guard
A reflecting pool crossed by a stone bridge
A marble column topped by a bronze eagle statue
Nineteen steel statues of soldiers on patrol
questions.explain: The figures, dressed in ponchos, walk through juniper bushes toward an American flag, representing a squad on patrol.

questions.q: Korea is sometimes called "the Forgotten War" mainly because it did what?
options: Lasted only a few weeks before the armistice was signed
Was fought almost entirely in secret from the public
Received less public attention than World War II or Vietnam
Ended in a decisive victory celebrated with national parades
questions.explain: Its stalemated outcome and its place between two larger wars led many Americans to remember it less.

questions.q: Truman described U.S. action in Korea in 1950 as a "police action." What was the legal status of the war in Congress?
options: Congress formally declared war on North Korea within a week
Congress never declared war, and Truman acted under a UN resolution
The Senate voted down a declaration of war after long debate
Congress approved the war by passing a constitutional amendment
questions.explain: The president used his role as commander in chief and the UN call for help, a precedent that critics later cited in debates over war powers.

questions.q: Which general replaced Douglas MacArthur as commander of UN forces in Korea in 1951?
options: Matthew Ridgway
Omar N. Bradley
Mark W. Clark
Maxwell Taylor
questions.explain: Ridgway stabilized the battle lines near the 38th parallel, and the war then became a long fight over negotiated terms.

questions.q: The Battle of the Chosin Reservoir in late 1950 involved what?
options: UN forces making the first amphibious landing behind enemy lines at Inchon
The defense of Seoul by South Korean troops against North Korean tanks
A large Soviet air attack on American airbases in Japan and Okinawa
UN troops fighting their way out after a massive Chinese attack in bitter cold
questions.explain: Marines and soldiers withdrew to the coast after being surrounded in freezing temperatures in northeastern Korea.

questions.q: The 1952 presidential campaign promise by Dwight Eisenhower that helped him win was what?
options: To invade North Korea and reunify the peninsula
To withdraw all U.S. troops from Asia in a year
To go to Korea to seek an end to the war
To ask the UN to replace American commanders
questions.explain: Eisenhower said he would visit Korea, and the armistice was signed in July 1953, early in his first term.

questions.q: What was one lasting result of the Korean War for U.S. foreign policy?
options: The United States left the UN in protest over the armistice terms
U.S. troops stayed in South Korea under a 1953 defense treaty
The United States abandoned containment in favor of rollback
The draft was ended and replaced by an all-volunteer army
questions.explain: A mutual defense pact and the stationing of American forces became part of the Cold War framework in East Asia.

questions.q: Communist forces under Mao Zedong won control of mainland China in what year, shaping American Cold War fears?
questions.explain: The "fall of China" led to an American debate over blame and to nonrecognition of the new government in Beijing for decades.

questions.q: In 1949 the Soviet Union surprised American leaders by doing what?
options: Launching its first satellite
Blockading Berlin once again
Testing its first atomic bomb
Invading South Korea directly
questions.explain: The test ended the U.S. nuclear monopoly and increased pressure for a larger arsenal, including a hydrogen bomb.

questions.q: About how many American service members died in the Korean War?
options: About 36,000
About 3,600
About 360,000
About 58,000
questions.explain: The Defense Department and NPS list about 36,574 U.S. deaths in the Korean theater; an older figure of about 54,000 counted deaths worldwide during the war years.

questions.q: The Korean War was widely viewed as the first major test of what U.S. policy?
options: Neutrality
Appeasement
Isolationism
Containment
questions.explain: American leaders saw the invasion as communist aggression that had to be stopped to show that containment would be enforced with force.

questions.q: What did American Cold War civil defense programs like "duck and cover" teach schoolchildren?
options: To evacuate cities by bus once warning sirens sounded
To take cover quickly in the event of a nuclear blast
To dig trenches in family yards and cover them with boards
To wear gas masks to school during daily practice drills
questions.explain: The drills and fallout shelters reflected a fear of nuclear attack that shaped everyday life in the 1950s.

questions.q: The Soviet-American nuclear arms race intensified after the United States tested which weapon in 1952?
options: The neutron bomb
The cruise missile
The hydrogen bomb
The Polaris missile
questions.explain: The thermonuclear test was soon followed by a Soviet test, and each side built thousands of warheads.

questions.q: Which treaty of 1951 ended the Allied occupation of Japan and was paired with a U.S.-Japan security pact?
options: The Treaty of San Francisco
The Treaty of Versailles
The Treaty of Portsmouth
The Treaty of Shimonoseki
questions.explain: Japan regained independence as an ally in the Cold War and became a base for U.S. forces during the Korean War.

questions.q: Which rocket launched the Apollo crews that flew to the moon?
options: The Titan II
The Redstone
The Atlas-Agena
The Saturn V
questions.explain: Developed by a team led by Wernher von Braun, the Saturn V launched the Apollo crews that flew to the moon.

questions.q: Who was the first American in space, in May 1961?
options: John Glenn
Gus Grissom
Alan Shepard
Neil Armstrong
questions.explain: His fifteen-minute suborbital flight in Freedom 7 came weeks after Yuri Gagarin's orbit.

questions.q: Apollo 8, in December 1968, was the first mission to do what?
options: Land two astronauts on the lunar surface
Dock two crewed spacecraft in Earth orbit
Conduct the first American spacewalk in orbit
Carry humans into orbit around the moon
questions.explain: The crew of three read from the Book of Genesis during a Christmas Eve broadcast, and photographed the earth rising over the lunar horizon.

questions.q: When was the last crewed moon landing of the Apollo program?
options: December 1972
April 1972
January 1975
August 1971
questions.explain: Apollo 17 was the last of the six Apollo missions that landed astronauts on the moon.

questions.q: The SR-71 Blackbird, a Cold War aircraft, was designed for what?
options: Short-range tactical bombing of ground targets
High-speed, high-altitude reconnaissance
Aerial refueling of long-range bombers
Carrying paratroopers behind enemy lines
questions.explain: It could fly above Mach 3 and outrun missiles, collecting intelligence for the United States from the 1960s.

questions.q: Sputnik 1 was a small satellite that did what after it was launched?
options: Orbited the Earth and sent out radio beeps
Landed on the moon and transmitted images
Carried a dog into orbit around the Earth
Returned to Earth after one orbit with film
questions.explain: The Soviet satellite's signals could be heard by radio operators around the world in October 1957.

questions.q: Which animal did the Soviet Union send into orbit aboard Sputnik 2 in November 1957?
options: A chimp named Ham
A monkey named Able
A cat named Felix
A dog named Laika
questions.explain: The flight showed that a living creature could survive launch, though it was not designed to return.

questions.q: Where is the Apollo 11 command module Columbia kept as part of the national collection?
options: The Capitol Rotunda beneath the great dome
The Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas
The National Air and Space Museum in Washington
Kennedy Space Center visitor complex in Florida
questions.explain: It carried Armstrong, Aldrin, and Collins back to Earth and belongs to the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum collection.

questions.q: Why was the Lincoln Memorial chosen as the site of the 1963 March on Washington?
options: It was located beside the Pentagon
Lincoln was a symbol of emancipation
It hosted the Supreme Court's sessions
It was where the Constitution was signed
questions.explain: Organizers wanted to link the demand for civil rights to the legacy of the president who issued the Emancipation Proclamation.

questions.q: Who opened the program at the 1963 March on Washington at the Lincoln Memorial?
options: Thurgood Marshall
Martin Luther King Jr.
Asa Philip Randolph
Whitney Young Jr.
questions.explain: Randolph, the senior figure of the march, welcomed the crowd, and King delivered the final major speech of the program.

questions.q: How did the 1963 March on Washington influence the passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964?
options: Congress responded by tabling all civil rights legislation until the following year
It ended Southern opposition at once and secured a unanimous vote in the Senate
It forced Kennedy to withdraw his bill after the crowd presented its demands
The peaceful turnout showed broad public support and added pressure on Congress
questions.explain: The march alone did not pass the bill, but its size and calm helped turn opinion and legislators toward action.

questions.q: About how many people attended the March on Washington?
options: About 25,000
About 250,000
About 1 million
About 800,000
questions.explain: The crowd, among the largest demonstrations the capital had seen, was both Black and white, and the day was peaceful.

questions.q: In which year did the nation first observe the federal holiday honoring King, after a campaign led partly by Coretta Scott King?
questions.explain: The bill signed in 1983 by Ronald Reagan took effect three years later, and some states resisted for years afterward.

questions.q: On the 20th anniversary of the March on Washington in 1983, what was a main theme?
options: Opposing the Voting Rights Act's renewal in Congress
Celebrating the end of the Cold War arms race
Protesting the Supreme Court's school busing decision
Renewing the call for jobs, peace, and freedom
questions.explain: A large crowd returned to the Lincoln Memorial in August 1983, and the rally came while Congress was debating the King holiday bill.

questions.q: What was Operation Linebacker II, in December 1972?
options: A ground invasion of Cambodia by American and South Vietnamese troops
A phased plan to withdraw American combat troops from the south
A heavy bombing campaign against North Vietnam to press it back to talks
A commando raid to free American prisoners held in camps near Hanoi
questions.explain: Often called the Christmas bombing, it was followed by resumed negotiations and the Paris agreement in January 1973.

questions.q: What was the siege of Khe Sanh in early 1968?
options: A decisive French defeat that ended colonial rule in 1954
A communist attack on the American embassy compound in Saigon
A naval clash with North Vietnamese boats in the Gulf of Tonkin
A long battle around a Marine base near the border with Laos
questions.explain: The base was surrounded for months, and the fight was watched closely at home as the Tet Offensive unfolded.

questions.q: Which pair received the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize for the Paris negotiations, although one declined it?
options: Henry Kissinger and Le Duc Tho
Richard Nixon and Ho Chi Minh
William Rogers and Pham Van Dong
Dean Rusk and Vo Nguyen Giap
questions.explain: Le Duc Tho refused the honor, saying peace had not yet been achieved in Vietnam.

questions.q: Boxer Muhammad Ali's refusal to be drafted in 1967 led to what?
options: A military pardon from President Johnson before his trial
Service in Vietnam as a noncombat entertainer for troops
A conviction that the Supreme Court overturned in 1971
A lifetime ban from boxing imposed by the Supreme Court
questions.explain: He was stripped of his title and license, but the Court threw out his conviction.

questions.q: What did President Carter do in 1977 for men who evaded the Vietnam draft?
options: Prosecuted them in federal courts
Granted a pardon to most of them
Drafted them into noncombat service
Barred them from voting for ten years
questions.explain: The pardon, issued on his first full day in office, did not cover deserters or those who were convicted of violence.

questions.q: What term describes post-war American reluctance to use military force abroad after the Vietnam War?
options: The Truman Doctrine
The Vietnam syndrome
The Monroe Doctrine
The Carter Doctrine
questions.explain: The phrase described public caution about overseas wars, and some leaders later said that the Gulf War had put it to rest.

questions.q: Which Southeast Asian nation was ruled by the Khmer Rouge after 1975?
options: Thailand
Malaysia
Indonesia
Cambodia
questions.explain: The regime was responsible for the deaths of well over a million people, while Vietnam invaded in 1978 and removed it.

questions.q: What led the American Psychiatric Association to recognize PTSD as a diagnosis in 1980?
options: Research on the trauma experienced by many Vietnam veterans
A surge in immigration from war-torn Southeast Asian countries
Studies of anxiety caused by the Cold War arms race
A change in the draft law that required psychiatric screening
questions.explain: Veterans' advocates and doctors pushed for recognition, and the diagnosis opened the door to better treatment.

questions.q: What was the effect of white flight from cities to suburbs in the postwar decades?
options: Cities attracted new industry as suburban growth stalled
Suburbs shrank as farmland around cities expanded
Cities lost tax revenue and population while suburbs grew
Cities became more racially integrated as families returned
questions.explain: Many white families moved out of urban neighborhoods, leaving many cities with fewer resources and sharper segregation.

questions.q: The "Second Great Migration" refers to what?
options: The move of millions of white families from Northern cities to the Sunbelt after 1940
The movement of millions of Black Southerners to Northern and Western cities after 1940
The arrival of millions of Asian immigrants on the West Coast after the 1965 act
The relocation of Dust Bowl farm families from the Plains to California in the 1930s
questions.explain: People left in search of jobs and to escape segregation, reshaping the politics of cities such as Chicago and Detroit.

questions.q: Cuban refugees arriving in 1980 in the Mariel boatlift numbered about how many?
options: About 125,000
About 12,000
About 450,000
About 60,000
questions.explain: Fidel Castro allowed people to leave from Mariel harbor, and Jimmy Carter's administration struggled to process the arrivals.

questions.q: The Refugee Act of 1980 did what?
options: Banned refugee entry from communist countries for a decade
Set a fixed immigration quota for each country of origin
Created a standard system for admitting refugees and for asylum
Ended federal funding for refugee resettlement programs
questions.explain: It adopted a definition of refugee in line with international law and allowed regular annual admissions.

questions.q: The Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act of 1980 did what?
options: Opened most of federal Alaska land to oil drilling only
Authorized the Trans-Alaska Pipeline across federal land
Transferred control of Alaska land to private developers
Protected over 100 million acres of federal land in Alaska
questions.explain: Signed by Jimmy Carter, it doubled the size of the national park and refuge system.

questions.q: Which requirement in the 1970 Clean Air Act helped lead to catalytic converters on cars?
options: A ban on gasoline sold in cities
A federal tax on miles driven by cars
A national speed limit on highways
Strict limits on tailpipe emissions
questions.explain: Manufacturers adopted converters to meet the new standards for pollutants.

questions.q: Where did the 1959 admission of Alaska and Hawaii to the Union leave the number of states?
options: Fifty
Forty-nine
Forty-eight
Fifty-two
questions.explain: Alaska came first in January, and Hawaii followed in August, the most recent states admitted.

questions.q: The Exxon Valdez oil spill of 1989 occurred where?
options: In the Gulf of Mexico
Off the coast of Alaska
Off the coast of California
In the waters of Lake Erie
questions.explain: The tanker ran aground in Prince William Sound, spilling millions of gallons and leading to the Oil Pollution Act of 1990.

questions.q: The Deepwater Horizon explosion in 2010 led to what?
options: A large oil tanker fire off the Alaskan coast
An oil spill in the Hudson River estuary
A massive oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico
A nuclear plant leak on the Louisiana coast
questions.explain: Eleven workers died, and oil flowed for months before the well was capped.

questions.q: In 1997 the Senate voted 95-0 against U.S. acceptance of any climate treaty that did what?
options: Allowed unlimited trading of emission credits
Required a ban on coal power in all states
Gave the United Nations power to tax emissions
Exempted developing nations from binding limits
questions.explain: The Byrd-Hagel resolution reflected concern that limits on the United States alone would be unfair, and the United States never ratified the Kyoto Protocol.

questions.q: The 1987 Montreal Protocol was an agreement to do what?
options: Cut carbon dioxide emissions from power plants
Ban commercial whaling in international waters
Phase out chemicals that damage the ozone layer
Protect rivers and wetlands from industrial runoff
questions.explain: It was approved by many nations, including the United States, and is credited with helping the ozone layer recover.

questions.q: Which president's state funeral in 1969 included a service at the Washington National Cathedral?
options: Harry Truman
Dwight Eisenhower
John F. Kennedy
Franklin Roosevelt
questions.explain: Eisenhower died in March 1969, and after services in Washington his body was taken to Kansas for burial.

questions.q: What was a major long-term effect of the GI Bill on American higher education?
options: It sharply cut college enrollment after the war ended
It brought millions of veterans into college and widened access
It gave colleges authority over the draft system
It replaced all federal student loan programs
questions.explain: Veterans enrolled in great numbers after World War II, and the law helped change college from an elite experience toward a mass one.

questions.q: What was the Berlin Airlift's role in U.S. policy after World War II?
options: It ended the Cold War by forcing a Soviet surrender
It led to the formation of the Warsaw Pact alliance
It showed the U.S. commitment to West Berlin without open war
It destroyed the East German industrial base
questions.explain: Supplying the city by air let the West stand firm while avoiding a direct clash with Soviet forces.

questions.q: The postwar Truman administration helped to rebuild which former enemy through reforms and aid, as well as the Marshall Plan for allies?
options: West Germany and Japan
Spain and Portugal alone
China and Korea after the revolution
The Soviet Union and its Eastern European neighbors
questions.explain: Occupation authorities, economic aid, and new constitutions turned the two defeated powers into stable allies in the Cold War.

questions.q: The International Monetary Fund and World Bank, born at Bretton Woods, grew from planning done during which president's administration?
options: Harry Truman
Franklin Roosevelt
Herbert Hoover
Woodrow Wilson
questions.explain: Roosevelt's Treasury, led by Henry Morgenthau, helped host the 1944 conference that designed the postwar monetary order.

questions.q: Frederick Douglass's life and writings were often cited by civil rights leaders in the 1950s and 1960s because he had argued for what?
options: A Black homeland to be founded in West Africa
The closing of the public schools in the South
Full citizenship and the vote for Black Americans
Strict limits on immigration from Europe
questions.explain: Activists saw his demands for equal rights as an earlier phase of the struggle they were continuing.
